The hon. member for Gloucester asked me about this matter on June 16, and since that time I have had the press report translated. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON NEGOTIATIONS FOR SALE TO JAPAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June
II	the Leader of the Opposition addressed a question to me with respect to a possible sale of Canadian uranium to Japan. I informed him on that occasion that I would discuss it with my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and there was an implicit undertaking in my answer to reply further to the question.
As the members of the house will recall, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I have informed the house on several occasions of steps being taken to promote the sale of Canadian uranium abroad. Among these steps was the negotiation with friendly governments of bilateral agreements for co-operation in the peaceful uses of atomic energy. Although these agreements do not in themselves constitute contracts, one of their purposes is to establish conditions, satisfactory to the two governments concerned, under which such contracts may be concluded on a commercial basis.
We have been anxious to negotiate such agreements with like-minded governments and have taken active steps in this direction. In particular, we have prepared a standard draft which could serve as the basis for these negotiations, and this draft was passed on last year to governments which had expressed an interest in co-operating with us in this field. Since then we have entered into negotiations with several governments, and we have kept in communication with other governments about this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: HALIFAX-STATEMENT ON REPORTED LAY-OFF OF EMPLOYEES AT CITADEL HILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 19 the hon. member for Northum-berland-Miramichi asked the Acting Minister of Labour a question regarding employment at the Halifax citadel. Since this comes under my department I thought I could give the information the hon. member was requesting.
The number employed at the Halifax citadel in an average summer would be in the region of 30 to 35 persons, and of those we keep about 10 who are employed on a year-round basis. Last December, as a means of relieving unemployment in the area, arrangements were made to add to that number, and as a result a total of about 70 men were employed during the winter and early spring. The winter employment program came to an end on April 30, and since that time we have been gradually cutting back the staff until there are now 46 on the job.
It had been planned to make still further reductions to bring the employment level about to that pertaining in a normal summer. However, in view of the unemployment situation in the area, and also having established that there is still useful work that can be performed, I have authorized them to keep on this work as long as the money in the vote lasts. I am sure hon. members will be pleased to hear that employees at the citadel who had previously received notice that their jobs would be coming to an end will now have been advised that there will be continued employment for some months.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Last Friday, Mr. Speaker, I was attempting to relate what the Minister of Finance had said about the projected expansion of this country under this government to the question of railroad construction in the north country. I was making fairly heavy weather with my French when fortunately I was interrupted by Your Honour at five o'clock.
Before going any further, I should like to give briefly some of the background to this question of railroad construction in the north country. I am doing this because from what I know, confirmed by an examination of the records railroad development in the Peace river country has been a sorry record of neglect, delays, frustrations and broken promises. It is quite obvious that one injustice has been done to the people of the Peace river country, and I hope to see that another is not committed as well.
The Peace river country is not part of the western prairies, nor is it part of the true north, but a connecting link between the two. Many of the people who went overland to the Yukon came through the Peace river country. The first white man to cross this continent came down from the north along the Peace and wintered close to the town of Peace River, then went on the next spring to the Pacific coast. I refer to Sir Alexander Mackenzie. I know these things, sir, because from my home, four miles from the town of Peace River, I can see the hill known as Mackenzie lookout, in the shadow of which Mackenzie built his fort. Along the
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin trail past my home went the people who travelled to the Yukon. There is a further grim reminder, possibly, that this area forms the natural gateway to the north in the fact that recently teams of archaeologists have been seeking in our country some confirmation of the fact that countless generations ago people crossed the Bering strait from Asia and so came into the centre of this continent.
In earlier times the large railway companies could or would never accept the fact that our country constituted a natural road to the north, both from the centre of the continent and from the west coast. It was necessary for the province of Alberta to construct railways into the area.
The province, of course, was limited by its boundaries and financial resources, but all during the 1920's there was a constant effort made to persuade the government of Canada and the railway companies to construct an outlet to the Pacific coast and also to build toward the Northwest Territories.
I have been able to find a great number of references to this, particularly in the speeches made by the late Mr. D. M. Kennedy, who was the member for Peace River from 1921 to 1935. He was supported by such members from British Columbia as General Clark, Hon. Harry Stevens, Senator McRae and John Fraser. These men were amongst those who had sufficient foresight to understand the necessity for the construction of this outlet.
I should like to continue, however, with regard to these promises by referring to a statement made by the then prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, speaking in Edmonton. The reference is contained in Hansard for 1926-27, page 2214:
"It is the policy of the government of which I have the honour to be the head to introduce a vigorous policy of immigration which will people the vast areas of undeveloped country in the great west," declared the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, premier of Canada, when addressing a mass meeting of the citizens in the First Presbyterian church last night.
The future prosperity of this country is bound up in the development of its great natural resources, and to develop these resources it is necessary to have a large increase in the population of Canada. There is to the north of this city a great tract of land that is crying out for development. The Peace river country is amongst the richest in Canada, but before the proper development of that country can take place an outlet to the Pacific coast is an absolute necessity. I pledge myself that as soon as it is humanly possible the great Peace river country will be given that measure of railway relief that will bring to the pioneers of that country the outlet they have been so long denied, and will open up the country for prospective settlers.
"The times that we are passing through are very difficult, and I would ask you to have a little patience, and in as short a time as possible, a railway outlet will be provided for the Peace river
1512	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin and northern Alberta districts that will open up an era of prosperity for that country which will not be equalled by any other province in Canada."
However, this was an election speech; and since it was a promise made before an election I examined the speech from the throne of the following year with some care. I had to look through it twice before I found any mention of the Peace river, and then I found this promise had shrunk to this insignificant statement; "that in due course steps would be taken to further colonization and settlement in other fertile regions such as Peace river". This was as far as the matter went. This is typical of the treatment given to the people of that area in so far as this allimportant question of railroads is concerned.
Now, as a matter of fact some survey parties were sent out, and they came back muttering about tonnage, population and economics. At that time we had only
20.000	people. Our railway tonnage was
110.000	tons going out of the country and
50.000	tons going in.
I recognize that we cannot be starry-eyed and visionary about this question of railroad construction, but I submit that railroads and their construction should be regarded as an instrument of national policy. They were considered in that way by the people who made this country, and I feel that the same consideration should be given today. If Sir John A. Macdonald and the people who constructed the C.P.R. had stopped to confer with hordes of chair-borne statisticians the C.P.R. would never have been constructed. Western Canada would still probably be a vast hunting ground for the buffalo or, more likely than that, we would have fewer provinces in Canada and there would be more stars in the United States flag.
In 1929 the Alberta government sold its railroad system to a statutory corporation created by the government of Canada. What was known as the Northern Alberta Railways was created, comprised of equal ownership by the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. By the statute of incorporation this railroad, the N.A.R., was authorized to commence construction of and given authority to build a railway to the Northwest Territories. The statute is chapter 48 of the 1929 statute. There is one particular part of the schedule I should like to read into the record because I think it has some bearing on what I propose to say. This new statutory corporation was authorized to lay out, construct, maintain and operate-
*-a branch line from a point at or near Grimshaw in a generally northerly direction to a point that will when surveyed approximate to a point in township one hundred and eleven, range nineteen or twenty, west of the fifth principal meridian,


thence in a generally northerly direction approximately parallel to the Hay river to the northern boundary of the said province.
That is precisely the route which we in the Peace river country advocate today. It follows precisely the same route which we advocate today on the question of this railroad which has been projected to Great Slave lake.
Considerable exception was taken in the house at that time by those who were interested and had some knowledge of the situation to the way the N.A.R. was formed. They said the creation of a statutory corporation of that kind comprising equality of ownership by the two great railway companies which were actually competitive was not a good thing for Peace river. Actually that is the way it turned out, because not one mile of railroad was ever built in furtherance of the suggestions made in 1929 when that corporation was created. It was actually left for the province of British Columbia to build this coast outlet, which it did when the P.G.E. was eventually completed into the Peace river country; and only a few days ago I understand the first train from the coast came up and across the Peace river at Taylor Flats in British Columbia.
The excuse of the major railway companies was that they did not think there was sufficient tonnage or population. I recall Sir Edward Beatty in Peace River saying that just as soon as our production was ten million bushels of grain, that would justify a coast outlet. Later on he was speaking in Edmonton, and I have here a quotation of his that was given in this house by Mr. J. A. Sissons, who was the member for Peace River from 1935 to 1940. Sir Edward Beatty then said what all of us knew to be correct:
That north country needs a settlement plan and needs it quickly, and together with that there should be a program of rail development.
The Peace River district impressed me most favourably. But its one major need still is that of increased settlement. I am confident that the country could absorb at least twice the population it now bears.
I certainly intend to suggest to the federal government that it embark on a broad policy of settlement for the north. Extension of rail facilities to go hand in hand with colonization. That is something that should be axiomatic.
We have reached and far surpassed all the figures that have been suggested with regard to population, tonnage and crop production. Our crop production is many times that which Sir Edward Beatty had in mind. Our population is four times that which existed at the time former prime minister Mackenzie King made his statement in Edmonton. Our tonnage going out is ten times that which it was in 1924. That argument no longer should serve as an excuse.

As a matter of fact I think we have ample confirmation of the truth of the statements our people had made earlier. As a result-and I think it is no accident that the two matters that have come to pass are linked together-of the projection of the P.G.E. to the Peace river country in the last two years, we have seen the beginnings of industrialization and growth. In the small southwest area of the Peace river country comprising part of my constituency and part of that of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson) there are a large plywood plant, two oil refineries and the beginnings of a petrochemical industry probably running into $30 million or $40 million and ultimately two or three times that much.
That has come about, I submit, as a result of the fact that at long last the coast outlet was brought to Peace river. I hold no brief for Premier Bennett, but I think it is only proper to pay tribute to him for the industry, initiative and intelligence he has exercised in directing that railroad into our country. I can only assume that it was because of the years he had spent as a member of the Conservative party that he acquired those characteristics.
We now face the question or the problem of constructing a railroad into the Northwest Territories. In that regard I should like to refer to a statement by Hon. Charles Dunning, who was minister of railways in the King administration. It was truly a pertinent one. This is what he said during those debates which took place in 1929 on this bill creating the Northern Alberta Railway. Speaking about this railroad into the Northwest Territories he said:
I believe I shall live to see the day when there will be a railhead on Great Slave lake tapping the resources of that great northern area.
This indicates what was intended at that time; and having in mind the countless numbers of people who went in there on the basis of promises of that kind, I submit it should be considered when we now come to deal with this question of a railroad into the north country.
Quite recently the government of Alberta established a royal commission known as the McGregor commission to inquire into the development of northern Alberta, which by the terms of reference was defined as being that part of Alberta lying to the north of the 55th parallel of north latitude. This commission has made a very extensive survey and I commend it to hon. members in so far as facts and statistics are concerned, though I must say I disagree very violently with some of the conclusions derived from these facts.
Included in these statistics is information relative to undeveloped agricultural area,
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin including certain territory which the commission designates as arable and other lands which are said to be possibly arable. I checked the figures with my own personal knowledge derived from almost 30 years' residence in that country and continuous travel through all parts of it, and I agree with their views which give a maximum of 14 million acres of undeveloped agricultural land with a potential production running into some $600 million to $700 million a year.
Certainly there is no doubt that here is the last great source of undeveloped agricultural country on the North American continent. I do not like cliches, yet the phrase "great inland empire" I think could nowhere be better applied than to this particular country. But empires, like all living organisms, must have nourishment and this empire was in grave danger of destruction, of dying stillborn because of lack of transportation facilities.
Following along the Peace river, the Northern Alberta Railways and up to the Northwest Territories, are people who for many, many years have struggled against tremendous odds to try to maintain themselves in that country. I say to the hon. members of this house, particularly those who come from agricultural constituencies, think of the problems of these people who have to pay 40 cents to 50 cents a bushel for wheat in order to bring it down to the railhead, $10 a head for cattle, $3 for other stock and so on. These are extreme examples, of course, and as you approach closer to the railroad the figures become somewhat less.
There is also the reverse side of the coin, and we must consider that everything which goes into that country requires an extra toll from the people because of the cost of transportation. We have every problem and every difficulty faced by people in other parts of Canada, but we also have this immense difficulty with respect to transportation owing to the great distances involved. On the economic scale there was slowly but surely being poured into the balance, the weight of these figures and if we had continued under the methods established by the previous administration there could have been but one inevitable result, stagnation and ultimate extinction.
That is why the people of my part of the country were so glad to hear of the program of national development planned by the Conservative party, as national development of course to us means primarily northern development. We were glad to hear of the construction of a railroad to the south shore of Great Slave lake, and to learn that we had not waited in vain for this railroad which, provided it commences at or near Grimshaw
1514	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin and goes through the Peace river country, will bring many obvious benefits to us.
I would like to mention the mineral production of the Pine Point area of the Great Slave lake region which, since it could reach the market at a cost which would make it competitive, would be a great step forward; but this is only the beginning, and there are many other tremendous considerations. The Northwest Territories would have the advantage of obtaining food supplied from an area comparatively close at hand which would substantially reduce the cost of living. The farmers providing these supplies would have a corresponding advantage by being able to increase their sales, and the new and expanding secondary industries of our country would find their markets increasing in both area and population.
The orthodox development of oil and gas would favour the route through the Peace river country, that is to say through the western part of northern Alberta. The figures given to the McGregor commission by the oil and gas conservation board of Alberta show as a minimum that 8,000 wells will be drilled by 1980 in the area affected by this railroad, at which time there should be an annual production of 62 million barrels of oil and 230 billion cubic feet of natural gas. This is a controlled production based on market requirements, and there are very interesting tables on pages 59 and 60 of the McGregor report with regard to this aspect of development.
The proposed route would serve 90 per cent of the people of northern Alberta, including those living on the British Columbia side of the Peace river, which provides the largest concentration of people and thus potential labour north of the 55th parallel in Canada, which I must say contrasts quite pitifully with what is believed to exist in the same latitudes in Russia. There is an excellent forestry potential with respect to both timber and pulp, and there are also first class hydro power facilities in the area to be served. The cost of construction would be reasonable, since there are no bridges of any consequence nor are there any substantial grades. Finally, having in mind the diversity of potential production, the railway would not be exclusively dependent on minerals which, being non-recurring resources, often cause the abandonment of railways and of towns.
The McGregor report recommended an alternative route. If this should be adopted, which I hope it will not be, I am quite certain many of the pioneer farmers of our country may well give up the struggle, which would result in a large exodus from some areas. I have recently been receiving an


average of 50 to 75 letters a day with respect to this matter, many from people I know personally as pioneers of the area, all urging me, as I hope they have urged the members of the government, to take these things into consideration when a decision is reached with respect to the route to be adopted when building this railway.
These people, and there are thousands of them, have held on grimly and tenaciously Dver the years in the face of considerable obstacles. They have cleared their lands, built homes and become good farmers- which they had to do in order to exist at all-and have also become good citizens. They have raised and educated their families, expanding the perimeter of civilization. So far they have done all this without too much help from government sources. They know nothing of national housing and very little of unemployment insurance benefits. For many of them some of the ordinary assistance available to agricultural producers has also been lacking. Even the benefits under the Can. Farm Loan Act have only recently been extended to some of the northern regions, and then only to a limited area close to the railroad. Despite these disadvantages, however, they have always held before them the hope that some day, somehow, at the end of the rainbow, there would be the construction of a railroad.
Many of us, of course, knew that a realistic appraisal of the national and world situation, so far as agricultural commodities are concerned, would make it difficult to justify, and indeed that it might be found impossible to construct that railroad having in mind only the agricultural aspects of the matter. We did however feel, as we still feel, that an additional incentive has now been provided by the further discoveries of minerals in and around the Great Slave lake area. We believe, therefore, that when the railroad is built it should be built through the Peace river country. We should not and we must not abandon these people. They must not be content to be second class citizens if they wish to remain in their country, or to have only one alternative, namely to give up their homes and everything for which they have struggled and move elsewhere.
If we permit them to leave behind them everything they have built up we shall be abdicating our responsibilities and failing in our duties. I suggest this railway is a fair test of what lies ahead in respect of northern development. Are we to consider human resources as being of paramount importance? Do we want to fill the country with people or are people to be subservient to the privilege and interests of those concerned in exploita-

tion? We are confident that the Conservative party, with its history and traditions-and this government has expressed its views by actions and utterances in recent months-will recognize our position and will appreciate that railroads exist to serve the people and not people to serve the railroads.
We have been told that a highway may be constructed as a substitute for this railway, that is to say a rebuilding and extension of the Mackenzie highway which now runs over 400 miles from Grimshaw to the port of Hay River on Great Slave lake. We welcome the fact that we now have this indication of the firm intention of this government to thus develop the northland, but I say this is not an alternative for our agricultural producers, who simply cannot develop farming communities at a distance of 40 miles or more from railway facilities.
As a matter of fact I am being a little optimistic when I say 40 miles, for I have in my hand a volume entitled "The Settlement of the Peace River Country", which was written by Professor C. A. Dawson, professor of sociology at McGill University, and Professor R. W. Murchie, professor of sociology at the University of Minnesota.
Their position as a whole strengthens mine. Here is what they have to say:
In the older settlements of the prairie provinces there are few farms more than 10 miles from the railway. Productivity fades before the twentieth mile from the railway is reached; beyond that it declines with great rapidity.
The McGregor report states that the need to stimulate agriculture in the north country remains open to question, and I assume that other people may entertain the same opinion; but if so they are not taking the long range view, as I propose to point out later. In any event I want to say that our agricultural economy is largely becoming, and will be even more in the future, one of mixed and diversified farming tailored to help us sustain our role as supplier of the Northwest Territories, as well as being geared to the exigencies of the larger world picture. Our people are realists, and the Peace river country has the necessary requirements so far as land is concerned to go into the type of production which will find and is finding markets, and we are turning away from the commodities which are surplus.
Such being the case, is it not a far better thing to do what is necessary to quicken the stirring of new life by opening this country, by establishing the many communities which will provide the necessary services along the new railroad through the country to Great Slave lake, than to accept the defeatist and narrowly pragmatic attitude which is inherent in this other type of thinking?

I believe that the appointed purpose of this land is that it should be made available for the many, a home for all who wish to come; and there will be many who will wish to do that. Any railroad construction and any development which aims at a lesser result is an abuse of the trust we have had bestowed upon us. "Without vision the people will perish" surely applies here, and this government has a vested interest in that phrase.
At this point I want to make it absolutely clear that anything I have said is not meant to suggest that the railroad should be built through the Peace river country without regard to the proper and natural aspirations and the development of the eastern half of northern Alberta. As and when, and that time may well be now, the economic development of that area and the requirements of Canada as a whole justify railway branch lines or highway construction or navigation improvement, then by all means they should be undertaken. But I submit as strongly as I possibly can that at the present time a branch line to the north which disregards the logical needs, and fails to give effect to the long held prayers and hopes, of the people of the Peace river country is wrong.
It has been said that the sole responsibility for providing communication to these people in our country rests with the provincial government, and I admit that it is a responsibility which Alberta must share, having in mind that the Northern Alberta Railways was originally constructed and operated by the province of Alberta. However, I would point out that most of the settlement came into the north country from 1912 to 1935, and that prior to the passage of the statute which implemented the agreement for the transfer of natural resources from Canada to Alberta in 1934, Canada alone had control of the land settlement. The homestead and land officers were those of the senior government, and the people who went into this northern area were encouraged to do so by the Canadian government. So the responsibility should be shared jointly among the province of Alberta, the federal government and the railway company.
Certainly the statement made by Mr. Dunning to which I referred previously with regard to this line to the north was accepted by many who went in there as a firm indication of the government's intention, and I know as a fact that many people who went into the north country did so because they honestly believed that this line would be built and that it was the intention of the government and of the railways to proceed with it. Certainly the department of northern affairs felt that way in 1956, because they presented a brief to the Gordon commission. On page
1516	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin 24 of the brief there was a map-I believe it was submitted by Mr. R. G. Robertson, commissioner of the Northwest Territories- which shows this railroad projected into the Great Slave lake area, and it shows it starting from Grimshaw. On page 29 of this report on the economic prospects of the Northwest Territories I find this:
A railway to Great Slave lake will not be just another railway. It is not a railway to a lake or to open a mine or to serve a community. A railway to Great Slave lake will be one of the great development railroads of the country. It will not bring population to the Northwest Territories to the same extent that the western railroads brought it to the prairies; but it may well bring in the years ahead a comparable increase in the wealth of Canada. This railway is quite different from most of the branch lines constructed in recent years which were destined to serve one mine, or a group of mines; its purpose is to open up a whole new region.
What I have said so far may be construed as being on a purely limited and local basis, but I submit that examined against the larger background of the national interest the answer comes out precisely the same. A branch line from Grimshaw to Great Slave lake would permit agricultural and other products from the northern and the Peace river country to seek their natural markets. We hold no brief for or against any particular area, but we wish to encourage our products to flow to the Pacific coast or to the east as economics may dictate.

speechtext:
Thank you. Some consideration must be given to the fact that the development of the Peace river country will lead to an influx of people and will to some extent syphon these people from the larger areas to which they have been attracted in ever increasing numbers in the last few years.
While I recognize that one cannot turn the clock back, and that the general tendency is toward people coming together in large cities, there is an inherent danger in this. In a news item in the Halifax Chronicle Herald of Tuesday, May 6, I observed a statement from the population reference bureau, a United States agency, that our neighbour to the souch is today suffering acute social and economic problems because the


population has grown quickly and concentrated in cities, and this bureau's reference points out that Canada is heading in the same direction.
I see no reason why we should not avoid this or at least minimize it, by encouraging people to go to the north country where there is the space and there could be the opportunity under the right conditions, based on proper railroad facilities. I am quite confident that there is still present in our people the spirit of adventure and the desire to make a new country that originally persuaded those from the older parts of the world to come to the new world.
Then is it not possible that in the final analysis the ability of Canada in the future to furnish food as and when required may be the deciding factor in the world struggle that envelops us? I would suggest that appeasement, not in the sense that^ it was used in the earlier days of Munich but appeasement of the hunger of the many millions who belong to the yet uncommitted countries, may be the answer to this struggle. We hear talk of agricultural surpluses, but I suggest that apart from wheat and one or two other products the normal increase in population, naturally and by immigration, may leave us in a position of balance in the not too distant future. In that regard the figures I have given previously indicate our potential, but you cannot make that production available as you would turn on a tap. There must be railroad construction followed by settlement, clearing and cultivation of land, providing of marketing facilities, establishment of communities to give service, and many other things. Even if the gleam in the collective eye of the Peace River people was transferred to the board of the draftsman tomorrow, I would thing that from 15 years to a quarter of a century might well go by before a reasonable percentage of the production potential is available.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I submit that it is not sufficient to build a railroad just to transfer large quantities of minerals out of the north country to be processed elsewhere, so that at the end of 20 to 30 years we may have only a gigantic hole in the ground in the north to show for it. I agree that mining is tremendously important and must play a great part in our development, but this development must be complete and well rounded, and will be a failure unless eventually it results in the populating of our country.
There is a phrase that nature abhors a vacuum. If we do not fill it we may well find that some other country may do so. Thus when we propose railway extensions

we should think in terms of 50, 60 or 80 years; and he will be a reckless man indeed who will say that based on that consideration the building up and settlement of a country like that which lies in the north, capable of a diversified economy, is open to question. Here is a great land, a fair and fertile country, stretching from Grande Prairie and the oil fields of Valley view in the south hundreds of miles northward to the south shore of Great Slave lake; a country which is capable of maintaining a substantial civilization and of serving as a natural and proper passage from the settled areas in the south of Canada to the great storehouse of the north. Here is a chance to deepen the present limits of settlement. We must not ask this country or the people who have helped to build it or the people who wish to go to it, to wait another 40 years.
I have good authority for this point of view, and I call to my support the statements of two great Canadians who at different times have stated their views in this house. Here is what Sir John A. Macdonald wrote in a letter to Sir Stafford Northcote on May 1, 1878:
I shall not be present; I am an old man, but I shall perchance look down from the realms above upon a multitude of younger men-a prosperous, populous, and thriving generation-a nation of Canadians, who will see the completion of the road.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier, speaking in this house with reference to the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, said:
We cannot wait, because time does not wait; we cannot wait because, in these days of wonderful development, time lost is doubly lost; we cannot wait, because at this moment there is a transformation going on in the conditions of our national life which it would be folly to ignore and a crime to overlook.

Mr. Speaker, before dealing with the subject I wish to discuss today, I should like to call attention to two significant events in the history of this country, both of which are taking place this year.
First I would like to call the attention of hon. members to the British Columbia centennial. When I was president of the Young Liberals Association of Canada, I had several opportunities of visiting that beautiful province, and was always impressed by the unforgettable scenery and the charm of the people of British Columbia. I therefore ask hon. members who represent that province in this house to please convey to the people of British Columbia our congratulations and best wishes.
The Budget-Mr. Rouleau
I would also like to recall the fact that this year we will be celebrating the 350th anniversary of the founding of the city of Quebec by Samuel de Champlain. A visit to that beautiful capital of the province of Quebec, that old historic city, is always a moving experience. As a matter of fact, it is one way of reliving the history of the beginnings of the colony. Quebec, with its monuments, houses and parks, has a charm which is equalled only by the hospitality of its citizens.
Quebec city authorities have decided to mark this occasion by impressive celebrations and, last Saturday evening, they opened the first of a series of events designed to commemorate the 350th anniversary of the founding of the city. Mr. Speaker, that occasion is such as to be of interest to all Canadians, in every part of this country, since it is on that spot that, 350 years ago, civilization, Christianity and French culture were permanently established. It is from there that discoverers and settlers departed for all parts of this lovely land of ours, Canada.
After the conquest of Quebec by the English, some 150 years later, our Englishspeaking fellow citizens brought over with them from England those various British institutions which we enjoy at the present time, including parliamentary freedoms. On the occasion of the 350th anniversary of the founding of Quebec by Mr. de Champlain, I would like to congratulate citizens of that city and extend to them my best regards.
I would feel remiss, Mr. Speaker, in not pointing out the immense contribution made by Canadians of French descent to the life of this nation. On the eve of the feast of the patron saint of French Canadians, I should like to mention that the history of this country began under a French civilizing influence and that we are now, as I said a moment ago, participating in a larger sense in the life of this country as a whole. I said a moment ago that tomorrow we shall be celebrating the feast of the patron saint of French Canadians. We will do so in a spirit of true Canadianism, conscious of the fact that our French culture is a contributory element to the life of the nation.
Mr. Speaker, I had a good reason, just now, to speak of the celebration of the 350th anniversary of the foundation of Quebec by Mr. de Champlain. It is well to recall that on the Plains of Abraham may be found two monuments, those of Montcalm and Wolfe, who are admirably expressive of Canadian unity, that unity which binds those two great

The Budget-Mr. Rouleau races which, in due course were joined by all those other groups of Canadians, of whatever origin they may be.
Mr. Speaker, on such important occasions as these, gifts are always in order. I would have thought that this government would have marked those two anniversaries by gifts to the people of Canada. However, the only gift they saw fit to offer us was the Fleming budget, one that will be long remembered. The first Conservative budget in 23 years, it is a deficit budget, a tradition with the Conservative system. It is the modern version of the great blackout years, and I would call it the "blackout budget".

In his speech the Minister of Finance has repeated the same old Tory principles which have not changed and which, as always, will carry the nation in the wrong direction. speakeroldname: Hon. J. M. Macdonnell (Minister without Portfolio):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to me to take part in the debate on this budget which is the first budget produced by my old friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). He and I had long worked together in the service of the party to which we belong. We entered parliament together in 1945. We shared a room for the first four years. I have watched with interest and admiration his progress to the position which he now holds which is based on industry, ability and reliability.
That was easy to say and to believe but from here on in it is not so easy. It seems to me it is difficult to support a budget-it is hard suddenly to shift oneself across the gangway-which has not been effectively criticized.
The attitudes toward the budget might really be divided into three classes. There are those who praise it and who are fairly large in number. I am referring now particularly to the press. Then there are those who are neutral, who do not wish to praise it openly but who in the phrase of a friend of mine praise it with faint damns. In their hearts they really praise it but they just do not like to come out and say so. Then of course there are those who really criticize it. I suppose they must be doing it sincerely but in the case of these real criticisms that I have run across, and to which I shall refer later, I confess that with whatever capacity I have for taking a realistic attitude they seem to be so far fetched and so wild that I can hardly believe they uttered them; though they uttered them, I can hardly believe they meant them. I shall refer to those later.
Of course it is perfectly clear that the budget was received with considerable equanimity and why not? It was merely putting into arithmetic what the people knew. The people had been warned in various ways. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) had said that if it was a matter of choice between debt and deficit on the one hand and unemployment and suffering on the other hand the choice would be made in favour of the relief of unemployment and

suffering. The Minister of Finance said the same thing.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I wonder if I might be permitted to ask the hon. gentleman a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Could the hon. gentleman give the occasion on which the Prime Minister said that before June 10, 1957?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No. I do not know that I could give the date. The Prime Minister has said that, I believe, both before and after June 10. Of course this was what Canadians voted for on March 31 last. After all, it does not make sense, with Canada's real resources, to permit a temporary world condition to condemn its people to want. As I have already indicated, the press had been pointing out that a slow-down was gradually making itself felt. Happily there are now signs of a turn-up. I should like to quote briefly from the Globe and Mail which said:
In framing his government's first budget, Finance Minister Fleming was compelled to draw a line somewhere between the requirements of an expanding national economy and a drop in revenues imposed upon the nation from external sources.
And again they said:
Instead of being a "sick budget", as described by opposition critics, it offers convalescent aids for an economy whose ills were aggravated by mistaken policies of the late Liberal regime.
Then the Toronto Star, believe it or not, gives the minister grudging praise.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. They said that
he overcame what they call "his prejudice against deficit spending in time of recession". The truth is that they had no warrant for believing that any such prejudice existed. But even that fraction of approval from the Star indicates something new.
I should now like to refer to certain signs of approval which occurred and which pleased me, certain signs that things were not as bad as might be suggested in certain quarters. I will read a few headlines, first from the Toronto Telegram on June 18:
Sharp Tightening Anti-Dumping Laws Aids Industry Here
From the Toronto Star, June 18:
Save Fifth of Mill on Sewers-Budget
The new federal budget could have "far-reaching effects" in long-term savings for Metro taxpayers on the huge sewage system program now under way,-

I read another headline from the Montreal Star:
Universities Praise Income Tax Action
I read from the Ottawa Citizen:
Removal of Sales Tax Helps City's Finances
From the Toronto Telegram again:
Applaud Move to Up Tourist Buying in U.K.
The article reads in part:
Ontario Hydro chairman, James Duncan, who served as leader of the Canadian Trade Mission to Britain last fall, today applauded the revision in duty-free purchase allowance for Canadians abroad as an excellent move.
I shall have occasion to say something more about that later. There was even a report-I cannot put my hand on it at the moment-that there was a good deal of pleasure existing or hope given to those who cannot speak for themselves. I refer to the dumb animals. Yes here it is. The Globe and Mail of June 19 says this:
Finance Minister Fleming may not have sent the farmers whooping with glee up and down the concession, but there was one section of his budget speech that seemed certain to bring joy to the hearts of the cows, pigs, chickens and the rest of the barn population.
To be specific, he said it was time the sales tax was removed from "certain agricultural, horticultural and forestry goods" such as "stock conditioners, condiments and food supplements for addition to poultry, cattle and other stock feeds.
In other words, it put a bit of flavour into things at the manger level.
I now want to come briefly to the speech of the financial critic. I rather sympathize with him because I have made some efforts in that line myself. There were the usual phrases that we have heard such as "bluff and bragging", "empty as a bird's nest". Then there was one interesting word that he used, namely "gobbledygook". I suggest that if he looks up the meaning of that word in the dictionary, he might be surprised at the word he has used and he might find it of some interest. I am not going to expose it here and I am not going to spend much time on the hon. member because I thought that the crashing broadsides from my friend the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) fairly well dealt with that speech. However, there is one quotation from the speech upon which I do want to comment seriously because the comment was made seriously, and I believe it is quite misleading. He said this:
One could certainly argue for spending and deficits, if they are not aimless but rather are planned, comprehensive and vigorous enough proposals to provide incentive, to provide lift, to perk up the economy.
57071-3-971
The Budget

Mr. Macdonnell
Now I suppose it is fair to assume that what the hon. member had in mind when he said that was the kind of thing which was used in the Liberal campaign, and I would now like to refer to some of the promises made. I am anxious to be very clear about all these things which were promised in view of the actions which have been taken since last autumn and the obligations which have been assumed by the government and which are included in the present budget which, as we all know, produced a deficit. In other words, when these proposals by the opposition were made these government proposals were in effect and have been embodied in the budget and, what was proposed was actually an additional deficit of $400 million. These are the figures which were bandied about and I believe it is very important that we should bear in mind that those figures were, and were intended to be, in addition to the measures which had already been announced, carried out and voted upon by the opposition last autumn.
It is interesting to observe that between February, when the campaign began, and the end of March, when it ended, things steamed up a bit and the promises, I thought, became a little more remote and a little less justifiable; in fact, a little more the product, quite obviously, of the excitement of the moment. I do not propose to go into details too deeply but I would like to quote from the Ottawa Citizen of February 10 last, where there was a headline saying, "Advances Plan for More Jobs in New Boom." We were going to have a new boom! Then there were all the other things-the marriage tax allowance, the basic exemption for married couples in the first three years $4,000 instead of $2,000; lower income tax; special reduction of excise tax on cars; aid for small business; municipal loans; highways; social security and youth. I will spare you the rest of the details.
On the same day, as reported on February 11 in the Gazette we had a headline, "Crash Program for Jobless Promised". The use of the word is interesting-it might have been a different kind of crash from that which was intended, but at any rate that was the word used. This is a Canadian Press item quoted from the Gazette of February 11, and it says:
His election platform-
This is the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), of course-
-outlined at a press conference was centred on an unemployment crash program-

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
But it included a wide range of promises from $400 million worth of tax cuts to special aids for cities and towns and outlying regions. It would appear, therefore, that my figure of $400 million was conservative, because this was to be $400 million plus. Then we get a further report on March 22 when the Leader of the Opposition was at a great party in Toronto which was described in the Ottawa Citizen of that date as a carnival. They were having a great time and, by the way, there was a really delightful and new idea at this party-six tax free weeks. A tax cut for six weeks. There is something very nice about that, something that attracts everyone. We all in our hearts disapprove of taxes and we all feel the world would be a much better place if there were no taxes. Here the Leader of the Opposition was going to give us six tax free weeks, and I am sure he felt he was really going to do something! It is perhaps fair to point out that this was done in what is described as a carnival spirit, for the newspaper said:
The Liberal leader announced the new pledge to rousing cheers from some 2,800 party workers gathered in carnival spirit at a Massey hall rally. Clowns, horn-tooters, bands, balloons, confetti and other stage gimmicks enlivened the rally as the 18 Toronto and York Liberal candidates were introduced.
It does not say that the Liberal leader was a clown but it says there were clowns there and horns and tooters and balloons and confetti and other such gimmicks. There is a sour note at the end; the reports says in the last paragraph that only one of the 18 Liberal candidates in this area was elected in the last parliament. Perhaps it is not very kind to remember that that one member is now cold and dead, and I think it is fair to excuse the Leader of the Opposition in the midst of all this confetti and horns and tooters and clowns. We should deal very gently with him under these circumstances and not be unkind.
There is one other quotation I would like to give, this time from the Windsor Star of March 14, which is headed, "Takes Aim at P.M." This refers to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), who was calling for tax reductions to improve the purchasing power of Canadians, the immediate removal of the excise tax on automobiles and the provision of missile orders for the automobile industry. I presume these missiles were to be used in the ordinary course of warfare and were not in any sense directed against the

Conservative party but at any rate this was his contribution to the situation. Some of these suggestions had as I said a romantic appeal; for instance the double exemption for young married people, and as I say, nothing was left undone to attract people.
These are the things which I presume the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) had in mind when he spoke of perking up the economy, and it therefore seems to me that we might have expected some of these proposals in the amendment proposed. But there was nothing to warrant that belief in the amendment. Where are all these ideas? They were not nailed to the mast and I imagine they have been thrown overboard by now.
Here is the wording of the amendment, which I think is rather an anaemic affair:
This house regrets that the government, in its budget proposals, has failed to cope satisfactorily with the problems of the recession in spite of the largest peacetime deficit in Canadian history and that it is moving towards greater trade restrictions at a time when other countries in the western world are moving in the opposite direction.
I will have a little more to say on trade restrictions in a few moments, but I feel that certain fellows of the baser sort are trying to exaggerate such matters. However, nothing in the resolution talks of any of this $400 million proposal. All it suggests is that we have failed to cope satisfactorily with the recession. They knew what we were doing and in fact they voted for many of the things we have done, so if anyone knew what was coming, they knew.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River had a good deal to say about the failure of the Minister of Finance to provide what he calls anti-recession medicine. I would like to say a word about that. The Minister of Finance, I consider, outlined very clearly and simply the things which might be done. He divided them into three parts and discussed them all-tax reduction, public investment and income maintenance. Let us look at these three divisions.
Firstly, tax reductions amounting to $178 million; public investment under housing, as the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) pointed out, provided for 100,000 men being employed under the far-reaching credit arrangements made. Housing, resource development, improvement in transportation; tens and tens of millions have been spent in those fields.

Then, again, there has been assistance to provinces and municipalities; and in income maintenance there have been increases in old age pensions, veterans benefits, unemployment insurance, to name only some of the things which have been done and in my opinion the Minister of Finance was justified in referring to this as involving expenditures of hundreds of millions of dollars, and he went on to say -and he was justified, too-that the timing was good. I think the timing was very good. If hon. members will remember, the housing industry, which had been lagging, was stimulated last summer and the results since then have really been quite remarkable.
Other things were done at the same time which prevented the recession going further, and I think that while governments must not take too much to themselves we are entitled to take credit for the fact that the comparison with the United States, for example, is now greatly to our advantage. Retail sales in Canada are ahead of last year, while in the United States they are 6 per cent down. Production in Canada is down by 5 per cent; in the United States it has declined by 12 or 13 per cent. I think that is a fair comment on what the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River had to say about antirecession measures.
Now I come to the criticism which has been made by our old friend the Winnipeg Free Press. The Winnipeg Free Press permits itself some comments on the tariff proposals which have been made by the government comments which-and I am trying to choose my words carefully-I can only regard as wholly irresponsible. There is an old adage which says that speaks of the person who given an inch takes an ell. But if you give the Winnipeg Free Press an inch, they take a mile.
On the one hand, the paper admits that "the immediate tariff changes are not large" but adds:
Mr. Fleming left no doubt that they are merely a start of what Is to come. Even so, they spit in the face-
This delicate language may perhaps result from the putting of heads together between the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River who used gobbledygook and the editor of the Free Press.
-of the British proposal to free and increase trade with Canada: they raise our tariff against one of the things-woollens-that Britain can best sell to us.
In one small move, the government has made nonsense of all the talk about more trade with Britain with which it attracted votes. Where we will be when it gets beyond the small beginnings is almost past imagination.
Now I should like to try to deal with these wild and irresponsible utterances in sensible
The Budget

Mr. Macdonnell language if I can. First, some comments on the facts of the tariff changes. All the tariff changes are extremely small-

speechtext:
Some are up, some are down. It is not quite clear whether the net result will turn out to be a rise in tariffs at all. As regards some important items- iron and steel, pipes and tubes and others- the result was really simplification and modification without any significant change up or down. They were also presented to the GATT signatories as a balanced package of increases and reductions and they were accepted as such.
The Free Press concentrates particularly on the wool tariff, as is to be expected. This industry had a special claim on humanitarian grounds. Yes, I repeat it, and I do not apologize for the word "humanitarian". The industry, as pointed out by the tariff board, which is not a sentimental organization, is by and large a small town industry. As the tariff board report points out:
Very often even today it is the industrial backbone of semi-rural communities. It is currently giving employment to several thousand Canadians . . . Partly because of its long association with scores of localities, it is part of the warp and woof of Canadian life.
I suppose it comes as near to being an indigenous Canadian industry as you could get. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate (Mr. Pickersgill) smiles, but I ask him to think it over. I make that statement seriously and if he will himself inquire as to the number of these small mills there are in small communities in Canada I think he will realize there is a good deal to be said in favour of it. I continue quoting from the tariff board:
Often in its own area it provides the only opening for skilled and semi-skilled labour.
This action is in accord with a statement made by the Prime Minister on June 5 to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association in the following words:
On the domestic front, the government of Canada cannot be content merely with a high gross national product. We are concerned, in addition, with the welfare of each individual citizen. The constant objective must be to attain for each individual his fair share of the produce of this land, and this can only come about in a condition of fullest employment.
Moreover, earnest attempts are being made to make up to the British the loss which will be incurred. A special concession to enable tourists to buy more in the United Kingdom without having to pay duty, will help in this regard.

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
In addition the Prime Minister said:
The tariff board's recommendations relating to wool fabrics involve a change only in the British preferential tariff. For the time being the present most favoured nation rates, as bound under the GATT will continue to apply. But it is our intention to renegotiate item 554b as soon as possible with a view to restoring the margin of British preference.
I suggest that in these circumstances even the most convinced free trader would find it hard to resist the argument, particularly in view of the promise which the minister has given.
I should like here in answer to the Free Press and its wild statements to recall, briefly, what the minister said about the broad trade objectives.
1.	To achieve expansion, diversification, better balance, and greater stability in our trade with all countries;
2.	To extend and strengthen Canada's trade and economic relationships with the commonwealth;
3.	To support and promote a regime of law, order and morality in the field of international trade; to respect the spirit and intent of international commitments; and to stand ready to defend our rights and interests if they are challenged or ignored;
And I should like to interpose here for the benefit of the Free Press to remind them that we in this party have welcomed GATT, supported it from the outset and regarded it as part and parcel of our economic life ever since. I go on to quote from the minister:
4.	To recognize the legitimate needs of Canadian producers; and to safeguard them against unfair trading practices;
5.	To promote the balanced growth of all sections of Canadian industry and agriculture.
Now I come to the second and perhaps even more preposterous criticism of the Free Press. In the same issue that paper charged the Diefenbaker government with what it calls "a great deception". Let us see what this great deception is. According to the Free Press, the Minister of Finance last December "refused to look ahead to the fiscal year in which the tax cuts would have their effect. Now, he says the principal tax changes affecting the present fiscal year were introduced and approved by parliament last December."
The Free Press continues:
They were made, but, as Mr. Fleming now admits,-
I think that is wholly incorrect.
-they were made without an accounting for the year that they, together with all the government's spending plans, actually affect. This is the great deception of which the Diefenbaker government is guilty. In the election it went to the country with its measures but without the bill for them.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

How far can captious
criticism go? On December 6 last the Minister of Finance set out the effect of the total tax reduction in a full year. In the course of his speech he also pointed out that there had been an increase of some $100 million in public service salaries. He referred to the effect of increase in old age pension, veterans benefits, dealings with the provinces, and gave the total. Moreover, the legislation involving the increases was passed unanimously in the House of Commons, and everyone was aware of what was going on. To refer to this as a "great deception" is simply a misuse of the English language. There is no foundation for it whatever. The Canadian Tax Foundation and any other intelligent observer was able to calculate with considerable accuracy the amount of the deficit before it came.
