The third criticism I wish to mention, Mr. Speaker, is taken from a publication for which I have great respect, the Financial Post, in these words:
One of the most astonishing assertions in the budget speech is that which, by implication, declares our export industries to be of little or no importance. And here we refer to Mr. Fleming's satisfaction with the continuing premium on the Canadian dollar over the American dollar.
The Financial Post attributes by implication what they call a most astonishing assertion by the Minister of Finance that he "declares our export industry to be of little or no import". All that the minister did was this. In the course of his statement on the financial situation he naturally had to deal with the Canadian dollar. He gave a simple, straightforward statement pointing out the advantages and disadvantages to exporters and importers of the premium on the Canadian dollar. Here are some of his words spoken on June 17, 1958, as recorded at page 1234 of Hansard:
-a change in the external value of the Canadian dollar brings gains to some Canadians and losses for others. The exchange rate is determined by the interplay of forces operating in the exchange market through their effect on the supply of and demand for United States and Canadian dollars. While our exchange fund is used to limit the effect Df short-run fluctuations in these forces, we do not attempt to reverse persistent market trends.
Could a more matter of fact, detached, realistic statement of the situation be imagined? And yet the newspaper permits itself to read into this statement a declaration that our export industries are of little or no importance.
I wish to add a word about the Canadian dollar. The Canadian dollar was set free in 1950 without any serious question being raised either inside parliament or out. The compelling reason was that with the heavy influx of money from outside Canada it was found extremely difficult to control speculation in Canadian funds and the financial authorities felt in these circumstances it was in Canada's best interest to set the dollar free. So far as I can ascertain, since then there has been no request from any responsible Canadian quarter that the dollar should be again pegged. I leave the matter there. I can only hope that the Financial Post for which I have great respect will recede from the position it has taken.
And now just a word or two about the recent speech of the hon. member for As-siniboia (Mr. Argue). What a grand time the hon. member had the other day in speaking in the budget debate. What free wheeling, slashing and swashbuckling! He really had a gale behind him with all the sails full and drawing well. I am sure he enjoyed
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell himself. If I may mix sail and steam I would comment that he was under such a full head of steam that I shall not attempt to follow him in his headlong career. I will quote only one of his hyperboles as recorded at page 1470 of Hansard of June 20, 1958:
I had expected until a very few weeks ago . . . that the government would continue for some time on the road it took last session, a road of progressive legislation, a road to improve the economic lot of the ordinary people of the country.
I must thank the hon. member for As-siniboia for those kind words. I think I should read that sentence again:
I had expected until a very few weeks ago . . . that the government would continue for some time on the road it took last session, a road of progressive legislation, a road to improve the economic lot of the ordinary people of the country.
I regret that the hon. member for Assini-boia is not in his seat to accept my thanks for his accurate description of the legislative program of this government. However, he went on to say:
But I have been fooled. They have now halted that forward progress. . . . Last session we saw the progressive face of the Progressive Conservative party but now we see the conservative face, the Tory face with the mask off.
What fun the hon. member must have had saying that. The name of our party is a double-barrelled name and the hon. member could not resist the temptation of making a contrast. I am sure it pleased him and his colleagues.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What he said is quite true, you know.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am coming to that in a moment and after you have heard what I am going to suggest I believe you will change your mind about that.
I am glad that the hon. member for Assiniboia felt that last autumn we were on the road of progressive legislation. I would suggest to him that this change which he describes so dramatically is a change only in his own mind. Let the hon. member go and read the speech from the throne delivered on May 12 last. He will find that it is still full of progressive legislation, that it is still the intention of this government to improve the economic lot of the ordinary people of the country. As I have said, I suppose our double-barreled name intrigued him and drew him on to make that statement in which he really accused us of having a split personality. The Conservative party does not have a split personality. In spite of his fulminations the hon. member does have moments of realism

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell and I suggest that if he will take the cure I have prescribed for him he will come back and say that his wild statements were not justified.
I have been advised that my time has almost expired-perhaps I have become too enthusiastic, too,-but I wish to speak about the commonwealth conference about which a great deal has been said in this house. I want to recall that on March 27, 1957, the present Prime Minister asked the then prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, who had just returned from a meeting in Bermuda with President Eisenhower and Mr. Macmillan-and I think Sir David Eccles and Mr. C. D. Howe the then minister of trade and commerce were in attendance too-if there had been any discussion of a trade and economic conference and the answer was highly unsatisfactory. The then prime minister indicated that apparently Mr. Macmillan had some idea concerning a conference to be called in London but as far as one could judge from reading the record it had not greatly excited Mr. St. Laurent. It did not seem to mean very much to him.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: His time is almost up.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Surely the hon. gentleman recalls that that proposed prime ministers' conference was not an economic conference at all.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I tried to make clear what Mr. St. Laurent said about the views of Mr. Macmillan and I submit that no one reading the record would come away with the feeling that Mr. St. Laurent was interested in the proposal for the holding of a commonwealth economic conference. But what about our present Prime Minister? The present Prime Minister was sworn in on June 21 and on June 23 he went to London to attend the prime ministers' commonwealth conference. I would like to recall what Mr. Macmillan said in this room just ten days ago as recorded at page 1150 of Hansard of June 13, 1958. Addressing the Prime Minister, the prime minister of the United Kingdom said:
-you came post haste from a general election to the commonwealth prime ministers' conference.
I shall always admire the way in which you arrived almost at a day's notice.
That is quite true. He continued:
Nor can I forget that at that conference by your inspiration and persistence there were sown the seeds of the commonwealth trade and economic conference to which we are looking forward with such high hopes.
Although my time is short I want to say that the preparations for that conference are


being pursued with the greatest energy. The Minister of Finance has been holding meetings of ministers and senior civil servants. There has been a preliminary meeting in London at which civil servants from all over the commonwealth have been taking part. There is no doubt but that this proposition has been considered in the most serious way. I am sorry I have not time to say more about it but I would like to go on to my conclusion.
I believe this is a good budget and when people look back on it they will realize that it was a compound of cautious realism and temperate and constructive courage. That is what I believe and I believe in their hearts that is what other people believe. I would suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that they realize it was a very good thing that their promise of a $400 million larger deficit was not taken up by the Canadian people.
I would also like to say that in this budget there is optimism but there is also wise warning. The minister said in his closing paragraph at page 1250 of Hansard:
But we live in a world of realities.
Moreover, I confess my concern over costs of production and prices in Canada. Only by keeping our costs of production in line with those of our competitors can we hope to achieve expanding employment and progressive improvement in our standard of living.
Farther on the minister said:
I echo the warnings issued by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to all sections of the Canadian people in appealing to all, whether employers, employees or self-employed, to have regard for the general interest in the returns they seek for their services and products. One must depend upon the sense of responsibility of free men and women not to demand more than their fair share of the national income.
He then went on to proclaim the fact that the role of government is limited, and that in a democracy the burden comes down squarely on the shoulders of every individual citizen. I believe the Minister of Finance has shown us the way to work through our present difficulties and to emerge on a new level where we shall be able to resume the advance temporarily interrupted.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I deal with some of the matters that are contained in the address of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) I want to take half a minute to say something else to the minister. I express the hope that before he grants any further financial aid to this fair capital city of Ottawa, or to the federal district commission, he take serious note of the warning that the hon. member for Assi-niboia (Mr. Argue) and I sounded in this house last week when we appealed for the abolition of firetraps in this city. I regret

very much to read in this morning's newspaper that yet another human life has been lost because of fire in the slums of Ottawa within a stone's throw of the beautiful parliament hill. I feel it is very poor policy indeed for the minister to want to spend millions of dollars to build a beautiful green belt around Ottawa when the heart of the city is in such urgent need of redevelopment and renovation.
On Monday last I had the privilege of spending a day in the most beautiful part of Canada, the lower mainland of British Columbia. Because of the kindness of the soviet ambassador in Ottawa a number of members of parliament were finally put on a par with the members from Ontario and Quebec in that we for once were able to spend a weekend at home. However, when I was at home I was profoundly shocked to find, at this very early date after the election, the extent to which this government had already lost the confidence of those who had voted for it as late as March 31 last. We have previously warned in this house that this new government which was elected with such an unprecedented majority was in this position. The expectations of action on the part of this government were higher in the minds of the people than they had ever been in any government in Canadian history. Because those expectations were so high therein might lie the reason for some of the disappointment nf the people at the present time. Now that they have read about the budget the disappointment will be even worse. Perhaps it was reflected in the results of the election on Monday last in the province of Manitoba, where the Campbell government held much firmer than most Canadians had expected it to hold, where the C.C.F. representation in that house was increased by more than 100 per cent and the Conservative vote in the course of 11 short weeks was sliced in half, and all this despite the very hard efforts of all the Manitoba members in this House of Commons, who left the ship of state at Ottawa to take part in that election campaign. I know they will faithfully record their absenteeism when they collect their wages at the end of this month.
While in British Columbia I spoke to the farmers there. They are disappointed. They are disappointed because as a floor price is established for one commodity after another it is becoming obvious to them that they are going to be guaranteed 80 per cent of the income they had been receiving. The government's promise of last session that the greatest regard would be paid to the cost of production seems to be entirely ignored in the floor prices that are being set up. Our unemployed are still unemployed. I believe
The Budget-Mr. Regier this week the supplementary insurance benefits expire. Our unemployed are now faced with the unpleasant and humiliating task of becoming wards of public or private charity, or of becoming a burden on their local municipal relief officers. It is no longer good enough for this Conservative government to say that the Liberals are to blame for the present high level of unemployment.
This past week the Tory party celebrated its first year in office, and after one full year in office the unemployed of Canada are no longer satisfied with the Tory government blaming the Liberals for the plight in which they find themselves. For a married man with a family, with monthly payments on his home and taxes on his home which are growing each year, with payments for furniture, medical bills, and so on, there had been some hope in the Diefenbaker announcement that no one would suffer because of unemployment. However, they have been unemployed since last fall and if our government members think that unemployment insurance over a course of six or seven months in the case of married families will prevent suffering, then maybe they ought to attempt to exist on that measly weekly allowance for six or seven months and I am sure they would agree that they had suffered.
If those unemployed cannot find work in the summertime-and we are now nearing the middle of summer-what will their lot be next winter? The prosperity corner of the late R. B. Bennett is becoming very round indeed for the unemployed of Canada.
The small businessmen to whom I spoke were also filled with great expectation. We are told that the small businessman is now receiving the consideration of this government. According to newspaper reports it may be that the small businessman is going to be able to receive advice-I presume advice as to how he can run his business, how he can get more hours of work out of his employees or out of his family in the grocery store. At any rate, advice is going to be given, I understand, by a special branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
The workers who are now employed, and they still constitute the vast number of Canadian people, are living in constant fear that their services may no longer be needed. We see lay-offs in many industries involving thousands of men with many, many long years of service. I refer to railway workers especially. Some years ago the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) claimed in this house that the lay-offs of men in railway yards were completely unnecessary and yet now, time after time, he tells us that nothing can be done to help the unemployed railway workers.
1530	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Regier
Other workers are finding each day that the taxes on their homes and other costs of living are rising month by month. They note the net earnings of their employers, and yet when they ask for a share in the earnings of the corporation to meet these rising costs of living and to bring their wages in line with their growing productivity, they have not only the bosses to contend with across the bargaining table but they now find that even the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), at Winnipeg, has told them to hold the line. Even the Minister of Finance said in his budget speech, as recorded at page 1250 of Hansard.
I echo the warnings issued by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to all sections of the Canadian people in appealing to all, whether employers, employees or self-employed, to have regard for the general interest in the returns they seek for their services and products.
Now labour is fully aware of what that warning of the minister means. The minister, however, nullifies his own plea with the preceding remark to this statement when he says:
-but to an important extent prices are the result of competition among the various economic groups which compose our nation, each striving for a greater share of the national product.
Then, later on he says this:
This budget has been born of confidence in Canada's future, not blind wishful thinking, but unshrinking realism.
I wish the government would use a little bit of this unshrinking realism when it advises labour to hold the line in its dealings with employers. When labour is at the bargaining table they have to consider whether the corporation with which they are bargaining can pay higher wages and remain in business. Labour has to consider the effect that a strike might have on their own immediate families and on their communities. Labour has to consider the public inconvenience that might follow if they withhold their labour. Labour has to consider what bargaining power the organization really has. However, let us use some of this realism and admit that as long as we maintain our present economic setup the employer will charge all that the traffic will bear. If he does not, in modern day circles he is considered an inefficient businessman. All these people, our unemployed, our workers, our farmers and our small businessmen expected action to be outlined either in the speech from the throne or in the budget speech.
This budget is a typical Harris budget. I would not go so far as to say it was an Abbott budget. Somewhere along the line a few years ago the Liberal party lost its way and it became an ultraconservative party. Possibly


Mr. Harris was the perfect example of that. I find very little difference between the language of the first Conservative budget and the last one introduced by the Hon. Mr. Harris, the last Liberal minister of finance.
There is nothing in the budget that is really of any major significance for these people. Oh, yes, in the budget there is an announcement that we are going to borrow more money. The government is going to borrow $200 for every man, woman and child in Canada during this fiscal year. They are going to borrow an unprecedented amount. We do not oppose deficit financing, but at the same time we recognize it as a tool with which the capitalistic system can occasionally give itself a shot in the arm. We allow excess profits to be taken year after year. We allow the farmers and workers to be denied the fruits of their labour, and then things come to an end. Then we turn around and have to borrow this money back from these people who wrongly took it from the farmers and the workers in the first place. All that is left of the farmers and workers is that they must pay back the money and pay interest on that money which is rightfully theirs. Deficit financing is very decidedly not a socialist approach. If you did not keep denying the workers the fruits of their labour you would not run into this snag where you have to borrow back this money in order to get it back into circulation.
Before asking labour to offer any co-operation in the solution of our problem let us consider what has been done to labour over the past several years. I am always a little surprised at some of our Christians who wonder why the task of the missionary amongst the coloured races of the world is so difficult. The answer is not very difficult to find. The Christians entered the areas of the world inhabited by the coloured peoples, they exploited them to the hilt and then, by way of the Christian church missionary societies, used a tiny fraction of their ill-gotten gains from the sweat of the coloured man in an attempt to reform the coloured man to the Christian faith. If labour is supposed to hold the line, they certainly expect a little more than pious appeals to the employers of Canada that they hold the line. Pious appeals are just laughed at by these people when they meet in the board rooms. It is a sign of weakness today for a business administrator to exercise any compassion, to respond to an appeal of this type.
I should refer specifically to what the minister did say. I should like to compliment the minister upon the goodly number of admissions that he made during the course of his

speech. On page 1231 of Hansard, he said, referring to the past 18 months:
In Canada unemployment emerged as a serious problem-
The minister says that over the past 18 months unemployment has emerged as a serious problem, a fact that they were denying in this house last fall. In fact it was not until after New Year's that government benches began admitting the emergence of some unemployment. For many long months they intended to label it, and did label it, as merely seasonal or regional. Now the minister in his budget speech says that for 18 months unemployment was becoming a serious problem in Canada. Why did the Prime Minister not tell the electorate that before March 31, instead of informing the electorate he could assure them we were past the peak so far as unemployment was concerned. If anyone ever deliberately, at election time, misled the people of Canada, it was the Conservative party.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to continue my remarks and to turn to something the minister had to say as reported at page 1231 of Hansard in reporting on agriculture. He said this:
There was a moderate gain of one per cent in the volume of non-agricultural production, but agricultural output declined as a result of the smaller western grain crop.
We in this section of the house greatly regret the decline in our production. In the last week we had in this city a guest from India. In speaking to the people in Ottawa he again sharply reminded us that one-third of the world is always undernourished, that a further third of the world is usually undernourished and that only one-third of the people have enough of the things of life at most times. As long as such urgent need exists for the labour of our hands we ought to be engaged in all-out production.
At page 1232 of Hansard I notice another admission of the minister when he says this:
Following the recession of 1953-54 there was a new period of expansion-
And then he goes on to say this:
As a result, world capacity in metals, fuels and forest products was enlarged much more rapidly than demand, and Canada, an important source of these materials, experienced the full force of this expansion.
Early in 1957 many commodity markets moved into a position of over-supply. The doubts created by these particular developments began to affect the plans for further expansion. In particular, this

began to make itself felt in the resource industries, and as a mood of caution began to develop it spread to other industries. By mid-1957 the value of large capital projects being started began to run behind the value of projects being completed.
And then later on he says:
During 1957, however, the competition for loan funds became less active as the year progressed-
Here is another lie of the Tory party. The
Tory party has claimed that they were responsible for relaxing the tight money policy when this was not so. The minister in his own words at page 1232 gives an honest appraisal of the situation when he says there was a decline in investment for which he gives reasons, and that there was a decline in capital expansion. Then he sums it up in one sentence when he says:
During 1957, however, the competition for loan funds became less active as the year progressed.
The net earnings of Canadian corporations began to decline and there seemed to be an over-supply of goods produced. Alarm was beginning to be felt and there was hesitancy to further the productive capacity of the Canadian nation. Therefore money became available for other social needs of the people, and that is the basic reason why it is now easier to obtain money for the municipalities. It is also easier for individuals wishing to do business with their chartered banks to obtain money, and all this big hullabaloo of what the Tory party has done to break the tight money policy stranglehold ought to be thrown out of the window by anyone who knows anything of the movement of large masses of capital. I do not believe the minister can cite one single fact with respect to any action of his or of any other member of the government which has had any effect on the relaxation of the tight money policy.
On page 1232 of Hansard the minister has something else rather significant to say, which is as follows:
Expenditure on durable goods, however, showed practically no increase over the previous year, reflecting in part the slower growth of incomes-
This is an admission that labour's income is not the reason that labour's productivity was increased.
-but also the rapid expansion in 1955 and 1956 which was based upon large increases in consumer credit.
In various debates in this house we have attempted to warn the government that the consumers of Canada were being oversold in that their buying was putting them into the position of accepting goods for which they did not have the money. We warned of the dangers, and the minister now admits that the market in Canada was oversold as far as 31-1958-3
The Budget-Mr. Regier the supply of money in the hands of the consumers was concerned. He said at page 1233:
Corporate profits declined by 11 per cent as costs rose and markets became more competitive. Other investment income, which includes rentals and bond interest, rose by 11 per cent.
When we compare the plight of Canadian corporations with that of the unemployed we must recognize that the costs of the depression are not being borne equally by the people of Canada.
Then the minister does an amazing thing; he completely brushes aside the old Tory concept that progress within our country is the result of the personal savings of individuals. At page 1233 he refers to such things as depreciation allowances and undistributed profits as being part of total savings. He says that in 1957 business saving-according to his definition that is depreciation allowance and undistributed profits-as a whole was little changed from 1956, accounting for about three-quarters of total saving. Personal saving was down about 5 per cent and, he said, accounted for almost one-quarter of total saving.
The money for the industrial expansion in Canada does not come from the poor widow's mite. This money, by the admission of the minister himself, or three-quarters of it, comes from depreciation allowances and undistributed profits. For the benefit of the readers of Hansard, that means after the payment of dividends there was left depreciation allowances and undeclared dividends of some $4,500 million last year, three times as much as the savings of individuals.
On page 1234 of Hansard the minister says:
The rise in consumer prices offset about half the increase in average wage rates so that advance in real income during the year was about two per cent.
In this connection I would refer to a speech he made, I believe in Waterloo, some weeks ago, when he admitted that labour productivity has risen by 3 per cent per annum in each of the last ten years. Now he says that the advance of real income has been about 2 per cent, which means he is admitting that labour is not receiving its share of the increase in its productivity.
We in the C.C.F. group place the welfare of the people ahead of the welfare of our political organization. It is therefore with a great deal of regret that we see so many warnings which we have made in past years emerge as fact. These facts are now admitted by the minister. We would much rather have been wrong in our analysis of what has been happening in this country in order that our people should not be suffering today. We do however appreciate that throughout the budget

The Budget-Mr. Regier speech the Minister of Finance repeatedly admitted the correctness of our position and we hope before long he will begin to apply a number of the remedies we offer from time to time.
The falling off in the domestic and world markets has caused serious unemployment which has been realized by the minister, who has admitted that while we have expanded our productive capacity such expansion has not been accompanied by a corresponding growth in markets. The minister has also admitted that our social investments have not kept pace with and have been sacrificed to the rapid industrial expansion.
The minister further admits that any inflation we have had is still very much with us and that the danger can be a very real one if there should be an upswing in economic activities. He has also brushed aside the old concept that individual savings bring about the growth of our industrial society. While we appreciate his honest analysis we regret that the budget seems to be completely bankrupt of any proposals for successfully meeting our perplexing problems. In fact nothing is offered which is of any significance. The government offers to borrow in this fiscal year $200 per capita, and then turns around and offers by way of aid to the municipalities the grandiose sum of 35 cents per capita. In fact, all it is offering to the Canadian people, if added together, amounts I believe to $1.65 per capita. The huge corporations brush aside the minister's pious appeal and continue to charge all the traffic will bear and so far as the farmer, the worker and the unemployed man is concerned, there is nothing in the budget that will help them very much. The people sacrificed nothing when they elected this government but it is perhaps characteristic of human nature that people do expect to get something for nothing.
At this time of uncertainty, when a bold and imaginative program on the part of the government is so badly needed to restore public confidence, the people must surely realize, after looking at the budget, that this government is nothing but the lackey of big business; that the Conservative party found itself a good advertising agency, organized its circus, had a real clown as leader-

Mr. Speaker, I was referring to the part played by the right hon. gentleman during the election campaign.
For the unemployed, for the workers, for the farmers, and for the only real free enterpriser, the small businessman, there is no tax relief of any significance, no full employment program, no restoration of the domestic markets, and no program for expanded trade. The minister, in the budget, has admitted the evils that beset us. It is unfortunate for all of us that this government is either unable or unwilling to apply the remedies that are necessary. We do not want an economy planned for us by monopolistic corporations, we do not want an economy planned by any one political party, but we do want an economy planned for and by the people of Canada through the medium of a freely-elected parliament and government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the chilling socialist snow which has fallen in this chamber perhaps a little sunshine from Alberta will serve to dispel some of the gloom. It is a great privilege to stand in this chamber and take the time of this house to tell you something of that fine constituency I have the honour to represent. It is called Athabasca, a name which comes from the great Cree language, and which means "the place where there are reeds."
Athabasca has an area of 60,000 square miles and is situated in the northeast corner of Alberta. To give hon. members an idea of the size of the country, it is approximately the same size as England and Wales. The population, however, is only some 65,000. But these people are some of the finest people in the world. In the first place they are Canadians and in the second place they are pioneers. They are still pioneers. They discard socialist gloom and they look forward to capitalistic expansion. Three-quarters of

our people are engaged in agriculture, and they live in the southernmost portion of this vast area.
I do not wish to dwell on agriculture this afternoon, because it is well known that agriculture is the backbone of Canada's economy. The main trouble facing the people of Athabaska today is the lack of transportation. In this vast area we have very few roads, and the roads we have are very primitive. When I tell you we only have 24 miles of hard-top roads in this great area hon. members will understand what I mean. Athabasca is the gateway to the north, and if we are to bring about the future of Canada in the way it should be brought about, we need roads and railways. We also need air strips.
During my election campaign I found it necessary to fly to some parts of my constituency; there are no roads in the northern half, and the northernmost section has not even a railway. My returning officer was killed; he flew into a frozen lake in a white-out. A week later we followed him up into the same country and flew into the same weather conditions. That is not exceptional. The great bush pilots who serve this part of the country do this almost daily.	Wop
May, to mention one of such men, has gone to the great beyond, and today men such as the Berry Brothers, Milt McDougall, Shoemaker and dozens of others who serve this great northwest possess the pioneer spirit to its ultimate extent, and the people who are coming behind them on the surface of the earth also have this pioneer spirit. Men like this need our help, and they have needed it for a long time.
The people I represent come from every country in Europe and from every ethnic group in Canada. A great section of the country is still populated by those noble Indian tribes, the Crees, and the Chippewas. It is to these people that we who pioneer this country turn to lead us across its frozen wastes and across its melting muskegs in the summer. They still retain the skill of the redmen; they still retain all the hardiness which mixed with white blood has created that sturdy race of people the metis.
The metis are principally Scottish and French in ancestry. They pioneer beyond the roads; they trap, hunt and fish and today, with the development of the mineral resources of the north, we look again to them to man the canoes, to man the freight boats, to cut the timber and care for the white men who live among them. But they ask no handouts. Indeed, they scorn handouts. They are not looking for socialism. They are looking for a new capitalism, a capitalism which has had,
The Budget-Mr. Bigg
as my hon. friends opposite say, a shot in the arm from the Conservative vision. This vision is not a new vision, but it is a rejuvenated vision. We do not welcome the scorning of this vision. We should like to see all hon. members in this house getting behind this movement to give the northland the attention it deserves.
I said before that transportation is the main need of the north today. The first consideration is airports. We require airstrips throughout the north country and we need them now. I suggest that this may be one way in which we can provide immediate work to many unemployed men this year. We have airstrips at Athabasca, Mc-Murray and Fort Chipewyan. When I last visited Fort Chipewyan during the winter we landed on the lake but during the breakup season, a period of six weeks in the spring, and for a period of six weeks in the fall there is no proper place to land at Fort Chipewyan. Fort Chipewyan serves a local population of approximately 600 persons and for three months a year the only method of transportation, air, is cut off from them. If a bush pilot wants to land in this period he is forced to land in the main street of the village where the children are playing. The space in which he must land is no larger than the floor of this chamber and only a bush pilot could land there. When he takes off again he does so at great risk to life and limb.
The railway ends at Waterways which is some three miles from McMurray. It is a joint venture of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways called the Northern Alberta Railway and most of the heavy freight not carried by air is brought over this line. It is proposed to extend this line roughly straight north to a point on Great Slave lake called Pine Point. At Great Slave lake the standard method of transportation to the deep north is by water.
It is not proposed at present to extend the railway further. You heard my colleague making a strong plea that this railroad should start in the Peace river district and go to Great Slave lake and I make a similar plea that the railway should be extended north from McMurray to serve this same area. It is not just a question of whether the railroad should go north out of Peace river or north out of McMurray if we take into consideration the future of the northland because the Peace river district needs a railway and so does the territory north of McMurray. My own suggestion would be to extend the railroad north to serve those portions of the Peace river district which already require a railway and to construct a

The Budget-Mr. Bigg
bridge across the Athabasca river at Mc-Murray and extend the Northern Alberta Railway northwards. I see no reason why northern Alberta cannot support two such railway lines. At present the railway companies admit there is enough tonnage going in and out of the north to justify the construction of one of these lines. I think it requires little imagination to see that this great territory could support two railway communications into the north if indeed not more than two.
Just north of McMurray there are tar sand deposits known as the Athabasca tar sands in which nature has deposited not less than 200 billion barrels of oil. This oil is not commercially available at present to compete with oil produced from wells but scientists have found the secret of releasing this oil and there is no doubt that in the near future this will prove to be one of the most valuable oil reserves in the world. Some sections of these sand deposits contain asphalt in a state where the asphalt can be rolled directly on the road surfaces prepared for black top. I have seen places where this has actually been used for sidewalks and short pieces of pavement and it has withstood the ravages of time and wear for 20 years. The asphalt was merely dug directly out of open pits and rolled on the ground. It might be that the government would put money into the development of tar sand for these purposes and build the roads that are needed in that part of the country outward from the tar sand deposits instead of building expensive roads inward from southern industrialized areas of civilization.
The Athabasca constituency is served by the mightly Athabasca river, one of the finest sources of fresh water on the North American continent. It is safe to say that the Athabasca river can supply any type of industry with water it might require in any amount for many many years. A fine fresh water supply is something that is required by industry today. The town of Athabasca is ideally situated for expanding into the chemical, oil and gas refining industries.
Roads are needed throughout the constituency. The great airport of Cold Lake is situated at the eastern edge of the Athabasca constituency where there is located Canada's only weapon trained range for aircraft and guided missiles. This great airport employs 5,000 personnel. It is in many ways the most up to date airport in the world and need I say that the personnel who operate this base are the finest air force in the world. We depend on these boys for the safety of this whole continent. It is here they are trained and here they live. Canada's pioneers of outer space will be trained here.

We need a road between Edmonton and Cold Lake. In fact, I would take up even more time than did the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) if I were to detail the roads that are required in this area because they are as numerous as the requirements for wharves around the shores of Newfoundland. We do not ask for all these roads. Roads are principally a matter of provincial jurisdiction but roads which lead to the north and to great centres of national defence may well be considered projects worthy of assistance from the federal government.
Athabasca is rich in her natural resources but her greatest resource is the people who live there. They are not discouraged by any difficulties they encounter. They have the same thrust and desire to carve out individual careers for themselves as had the first pioneers to this country. They are not whiners but workers. Again I say they look to us for help. Before them is the great north country and behind them the rich plains of Alberta. I know they are not going to be disappointed in the help we give them. There is one last great frontier in Canada, the north. We who live at the gate to the north challenge the youth of Canada to move in and possess that great northland.
There will be no handouts; there will be work; there will be struggle. I assure you that there will be great reward.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like to begin by congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) upon one aspect, and upon one aspect only, of his presentation of the budget the other evening. I do think that the Minister of Finance gave evidence the other evening of what might be called the first stage in the education of Donald Fleming. I contrasted it, as I am sure every other hon. member who was here a year ago did, with the forecast of this first budget that he gave to the press and which appeared in the Ottawa Journal on June 26 last, almost a year ago. That was the day the minister, after five days in office, said that a new budget to reduce taxes and increase old age pensions would be brought down in the fall. This was in black type, as it was obviously considered by the reporter to be the most important of the many important forecasts that the minister made at that time. I will not use a word that might cause commotion in the house, Mr. Speaker, but we all know that we never saw that budget. We also know that-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You saw tax reduction.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You saw increases in old age pensions.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We saw the increase in old age pensions; we saw a lot of things. We have seen the most phenomenal increase in deficits in the history of Canada in peace time.
I may say, sir, the minister also promised us at that time that he had declared war on waste and extravagance. We have seen the results of the first battle-I suppose that is the first battle of the war on waste and extravagance-we have the greatest estimates for expenditures ever presented by any Canadian government to any parliament.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which one are you opposed to?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The next thing that I would like particularly to refer to is that we heard none of the things in the minister's speech that we heard so frequently in the past from the minister and this is why I say it seems to me that the minister's speech represents a stage in the education of a minister of finance. There is not a word in his speech about how he had changed the tight money policy; there is not really anything about that policy at all. There is not a word about the savings the minister had effected by the elimination of waste and extravagance. There is not a word about the so-called over-taxation which was one of the most appealing- I suppose one of the most appealing-features of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Diefenbaker) great appeal a year ago when the Prime Minister told us that we were overtaxed by over $500 million a year. Presumably, if we were overtaxed-and not "presumably" because the Prime Minister worked it all out arithmetically-that $500 million was going to be reduced. Well, of course, it has not been; it is not going to be. There was not a word either about that so-called hidden report that the Prime Minister made such a fuss about here last January in the previous parliament.
Indeed, we find that the Minister of Finance attributed the unemployment to something entirely different from the policies of the Liberal government. In his speech he attributed the unemployment to world causes. Indeed, nothing is more remarkable, it seems to me, in the minister's speech than the remarkable tribute he paid in the first part of his speech to the accuracy of his predecessor's economic forecast. In order to make sure that my memory was not playing any tricks on me I sent for Mr. Harris' budget speech, and I have made a comparison of that section of his speech with the minister's speech and the amazing thing is that practically the whole of Mr. Harris' forecasts
The Budget-Mr. Pickersgill were borne out by the experience of the year which has now been completed. His estimates of the gross national product, his estimates of the probable decline, which he very honestly forecast, in the rate of advance and his estimate that there would be an advance all through the year were completely borne out; his estimate that there would be an increase in employment was borne out. Indeed, it would have been hard to conceive of any more completely accurate vindication through the year 1957 of the forecasts made in Mr. Harris' budget than are found in the accounts produced by the minister in certain paragraphs of his speech.
It is evidently the strategy now to leave all these political arguments to the lesser lights. We had all the claptrap that we used to hear from the minister regurgitated by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell). It is apparently no longer quite respectable for a minister of finance to talk such nonsense but for an aspirant to that office it was apparently regarded as good coin.
Perhaps you will call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I had just paid a compliment to the hon. member for Carleton. I was astonished at the pattern which seemed to appear in this debate from the other side of the house this afternoon, when the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), followed the same extraordinary line taken by the hon. member for Carleton the other day. This extraordinary, and I might say rather belated interest of hon. gentlemen opposite in the program of the Liberal party in the last election, is very touching to us on this side of the house. The only conceivable reason I have been able to think of for this extraordinary interest in that program at this stage is that hon. gentlemen opposite are executing still another diversion in this debate. They realize the damp squib that this budget is turning out to be, and they are trying to distract public attention from the budget to something else. I do not intend to pursue them in this diversionary line.
I am much more tempted to pursue another line, but I intend to resist that temptation, too. The line I should like to pursue if the clock was not working against me is the line about unemployment. The hon. member for Carleton repeated all the old pre-election

The Budget-Mr. Pickersgill explanations about unemployment. However, the minister was honest enough in his budget speech to say nothing whatever about any of those so-called explanations. The minister instead said that we did not have as much unemployment as other people had but that unemployment was a world-wide condition. I am not surprised that he did not use the old line, because if he did not remember it himself his officials probably reminded him that as late as November he was telling people there was no serious unemployment.
I would, rather, deal with two specific points in connection with this budget. The other day the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), in a display of candour and naivete that was, I think, very entertaining and interesting, admitted, and I give him credit for his honesty, that he had been fooled by the progressive face, I think he called it, of hon. gentlemen opposite. He later used the word "mask". Now we in this party never thought it was a progressive face; we always knew it was a mask and we were at no time deceived. It does seem to me, that the progressive mask on the Tory face is better illustrated by the trade proposals in the budget than by any other aspect of it, although I think almost any aspect of it could be taken to illustrate the same point.
There does seem to be something peculiar about this country. Once in every generation it seems to be necessary for the people of Canada to learn the same lesson. We had it in 1911; we had it in 1930; and we had it again in this dual effort of 1957 and 1958. Every so often it seems to be possible, I suppose because of the fallibility of human memory, to excite the people of this country by stirring up feeling against the United States and by parading a great affection for Great Britain. Now we had that in 1911; we had it in 1930, and we had it again in the last two years. In every case, sir, it is always followed by the same thing. The affection for Britain proves to be purely verbal and when it comes to policy, those of us who remember 1932 and what followed from it; those who remember 1911 and what followed from that, will have no real doubt about what is going to follow again. The pattern does seem to go on.
It starts, of course, with this wholly fallacious doctrine that it is a wicked thing to have a lot of trade with the United States. It never seems to occur to a real Tory that trade is an advantageous thing for any country. It never seems to occur to a real Tory that, other things being equal, any person engaged in trade will try to sell what he has to sell for the best price wherever he can get it, and buy for the lowest price wherever he can get it. I can assure you that
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
is one thing which the British, including the British Tories, never forget. But it is not long after the Tories come into office on any occasion when this same old reaction occurs.
It is, I think, interesting that, even though the mask is off, as the hon. member for Assiniboia has said, hon. gentlemen opposite, with the exception of the hon. member for Carleton, seem to be a little ashamed of the face. In 1930 I think you could say Mr. Bennett approached this whole problem boastfully. We had Mr. Bennett boasting about raising tariffs and blasting his way into the markets of the world. We watched for five years while the trade of this country shrank steadily and the prosperity and well-being of the people disappeared.
We have a rather different situation this time. If Mr. Bennett was boastful, I suppose the only thing we can say is that Mr. Fleming is furtive. The Minister of Finance tries to sneak this change in trading policy in by the kitchen door. I use the word "kitchen" advisedly because the hon. member for Greenwood this afternoon said these tariff increases were so small. Of course, they are small in exactly the same way as the famous housemaid's baby was small, as I reminded the house this afternoon. But a rose by any other name would smell as sweet.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are mixing your metaphors.

speechtext:
Yes, and with a certain deliberation which the hon. gentleman will perhaps comprehend later in the evening.
This proposal about dumping is the nicest example one could find of this furtive approach. The Minister of Finance, in a statement which was literally true but I hesitate to say, sir, calculated to mislead, and which perhaps may have had the effect of misleading, suggested he was going back to 1948. It is true, of course, that in 1948 Mr. St. Laurent came into the house and said, let us take off the statute books this provision that has not been used for thirteen years. The fact is that this dumping provision, this Bennett provision-I do not know that I should call it a Bennett provision because Mr. Meighen tried it before him and it was repealed once before by the Liberals before Bennett-is, of course, of all the protective devices, the most insidious and the most dangerous.
I well remember, in the year 1933 driving through Chicago and having two flat tires-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

-and having to replace them. Naturally, I bought in the cheapest

market I could find, which was Sears-Roebuck. When I came to the Ambassador bridge at Windsor, the Canadian end of it, there were five different imposts put on before I was through, and when I had got finished I had paid more in duty than I had paid for the tires. One of these imposts was described in such a way-I forget the precise words now

as to give the impression that the Canadian government was collecting it for the United States. I said to the customs officer, "You don't mean to say this is going into the United States treasury, do you?" He said, "Oh, no, but a lot of people think it is." I said, "If I were an organizer of the Liberal party"-and I may say that in those days I was a lecturer in history in the university and had only an academic interest in politics-"or if I were a member of the Liberal party, I would set up a booth at the end of this bridge and nobody that crossed it would ever vote Tory again." I had already been converted prior to that time, but if I had not been converted I certainly would have been by that experience.

didn't you buy the tires in Canada?

Bennett buggies.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The thing that astonished me most of all in the astonishing speech made by the hon. member for Greenwood was his suggestion this afternoon that the woollen industry was an industry indigenous to Canada. I really want to say something about this increase in tariff on wool because it seems to me that in many ways it is the most fantastic thing in the whole budget. Here we have a government headed by a Prime Minister whose main appeal to the Canadian people was that he was going to divert a great part of our trade from the United States to the United Kingdom. If anybody doubts that the Prime Minister gave that kind of impression, not merely in this country but elsewhere, I should like to read a brief extract from the monthly bulletin of the commonwealth and empire industries association published in London. It is commenting on the Prime Minister's great success in March of 1958, something which we all remember. Here is a sentence or two:
The Budget-Mr. Pickersgill
In 1957 the Conservative leader. Mr. Diefenbaker, roundly declared that he would like to see a switch of 15 per cent of Canada's trade with the United States to the United Kingdom. On assuming office he had not a majority sufficient to allow him to put his plans into effect and so he went to the country again in 1958 having made no concessions or abated one item of his intentions. The result we know,-
The result, Mr. Speaker, we know. The first result was this. The first time the Prime Minister has had a chance to do anything about it, what does he do? He puts on a tariff on what is-if any single item is-the classic export from Britain to Canada. It is true that the government say it is only a small duty, that it really will not increase the cost of what anyone has to pay very much. But I say, sir, that small or large, the symbolic significance of this increase is tremendous. In the first place, it is an evidence of the trend, the direction in which this whole tariff section of the minister's speech pointed. It is the first faltering step; but I suspect that, if the minister is able to get away with this one, there will be many longer strides following.
This is no matter of mere academic interest to anyone who represents a constituency where the majority of the electors make their living out of what is an indigenous industry and what is the oldest industry in this country, namely the fishing industry. Not only do my constituents have to make their living by selling in the markets of the world at world prices practically everything that they produce, whether it be wood products or fish, but they have to buy practically everything they consume in a market, which is in the essence of things- and always has been since confederation, since 1949-protected to a degree. It was not protected to the same extent before confederation. This tariff on British woollens will have the effect of increasing their cost of living, perhaps not very much but some.
But what I think is much more serious to Newfoundland is the second part of the minister's proposal, namely the proposal that he is also going to increase, if he can worm out of our trade agreements, the most-favoured-nation tariff. Everybody knows that outside of Britain the one country that has made real progress in getting into the Canadian woollen market is Italy. Perhaps everyone in the house does not know that Italy is without exception the best market for Newfoundland fish on the continent of Europe. There has been a risk, ever since the common market was established, that this market for Canadian fish may be lost to some degree because of the combined tariff around these six nations, because France is included and because France has fishing grounds at

The Budget-Mr. Pickersgill St. Pierre. But if we are going to kick the Italians in the teeth as we have already indicated we are going to kick the British in the teeth-I should not say "we"; I should say as the government has already indicated it is going to kick the British in the teeth- we are going to jeopardize even more that market for our fish and that will affect the interests of every fish producer, every producer of cod fish on the east coast. It is true that it is only Newfoundland fish that goes to Italy. But if that market should be diminished or lost, it simply means there is going to be that much keener competition for the markets that remain. We simply cannot afford to jeopardize any of our external markets.
I want to take the rest of the time I have at my disposal to refer to a great gaping hole, a great chasm, in the budget. I notice that the minister said the other night that he had-he interjected this when my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River was speaking-made some reference to federal-provincial relations in the budget. Of course the minister was right.

Additional financial assistance being given to the provinces will enable them to proceed with needed capital improvements in the provincial and municipal fields.
(Text):

Mr. Fleming said on this point that a new dominion-provincial conference will be called, probably this year,-
That was 1957.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I continue the quotation:
-to revise the basis for division of the joint fields of taxation-

-and to provide the provinces with increases in these revenues.

And what did we have? We had a two-day conference in November when the provincial governments were not allowed to discuss the main subject, they were diverted into other fields which most of them had not come there to discuss and about which the premier of Manitoba-and he is still the premier of that province for a few more hours-complained.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

This is not because I do not trust my officials but because I have no officials to do it for me. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In January Mr. Lesage and I did our best to get the Minister of Finance to state that he would stabilize his extra 3 per cent, and he pretended not to understand the argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He didn't pretend any such thing.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now he has admitted that there is no stabilization whatsoever for the extra amount. Mr. Greenlay, the provincial treasurer of Manitoba-according to my best information he is still the provincial treasurer -is reported to have said, according to the Winnipeg Free Press of June 20 last-I might say incidentally that when Mr. Greenlay entered the government in Manitoba he was generally considered to be a member of the party of the hon. members opposite, but he has learned something-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He certainly has.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What he is reported to have said is as follows:
The claims of Prime Minister Diefenbaker and Tory MP's who campaigned here during the provincial election-that Ottawa was giving Manitoba an extra $3.4 million in tax-rental payment-are misleading and probably false, Hon. C. E. Greenlay indicated Thursday.
The fact is, of course, that if the revenues from these great fields of taxation do diminish -as they are diminishing, and as the minister himself indicated in the table he put on Hansard he expected them to diminish-I suspect that he gave as optimistic estimate as he dared to give of that diminution-it could happen that this whole $62 million would be
The Budget-Mr. Pickersgill out of the window. Certainly the minister is not paying on the basis of the extra $62 million at the present time, or anything like it, and he knows that. He has never given us any estimate of what in his opinion it is that the provinces really will get, in the light of revised figures of which he and his officials are aware but of which this house is not aware. We do not know what they are likely to get, but it is perfectly clear that it is not going to be anything like the $62 million and my suspicion is that if there is any addition at all when the accounts are in at the end of the year, it will be a very small one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It will be 3 per cent more than they would have received had there not been a change from the Liberal administration.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did you use stabilization?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister is quite wrong even in his last observation, if I caught it correctly, because if they do get anything out of this $62 million it will be because Mr. Harris' stabilization comes into effect, and furthermore it will be only because of that and not because of anything done by the present government, if they do get as much as they got last year.
We have been told absolutely nothing about the future. We know that this famous dole, the unilateral dole by telegram, is for one year only, and we do not know what is going to happen after March 31 next. The provincial governments have been told nothing whatsoever and they certainly did have the right to expect that they would at least be told in the budget, because they were not allowed to discuss the matter at the conference. I must confess I do not believe the government has the slightest intention of meeting the provinces again in 1958. Alternatively, they should know what it is proposed to do when the present statute expires on March 31.
I predict that what will happen is that at the beginning of next session we will have another of these telegrams-I hope the arithmetic will be correct this time-covering another interim arrangement. This method will be used because the government has been too busy with other things to bother with the provinces.
If the government has different plans, if the government really intends, when they have disposed of parliament, to call some kind of a conference, or if they intend to work out some kind of hole-in-corner deal with the government of Ontario-as Mr. Macaulay, the new minister, seems to be hinting every few days with, I suspect, a little prodding from behind from the premier of that province- then surely this parliament is entitled to know, as it was always given the opportunity

The Budget-Mr. Pickersgill to know under the previous government, what is the policy of the government. We have not the faintest idea; there is no indication whatsoever in this budget as to what the provincial governments may expect after March 31, what they are really going to get, or even what the department thinks they are going to get or what the minister thinks they are going to get between now and March 31.
The minister said with great exuberance last June that the government was going to hold a conference last year to revise the basis for the division of the joint fields of taxation. There has been no such division. The government did not decide anything at the conference, but they sent out this telegram, just taking the formula of Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Harris and giving the appearance of adding to it another 3 per cent, but they left in the joker about stabilization so that the 3 per cent could disappear, as it is indeed disappearing and as I suspect it will disappear more and more as more realistic estimates come to be made as to what, in fact, the proceeds of these great fields of taxation will turn out to be.
It does seem to me that on these two grounds alone the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) and which I had the honour of seconding is amply justified in both of these particulars. The minister has said he has given this extra money to the provinces. That is a free translation of what he said in French as I read it a little while ago. He said he gave it to them so that they could embark on big spending programs. But he did not tell them he had done it all with mirrors, and that they would probably not get any more at all. In fact, he left them in a worse state than before he started, because they do not know what they are going to get, whether it will be more or less. My hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River set out the other day what was done with respect to the public works program and the national development program. There again, it was all done with mirrors. There is nothing whatsoever which will give us any hope of effective action being taken to meet the recession.
Of course, the minister talked a lot about the tax reductions he made last December. I have been looking at that, and I have added to the $178 million the $26 million allowed in the present budget, and it comes to a little over $200 million. This is all we got in tax reductions as compared with the half a billion dollars which the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance promised just a year ago would be the amount of the reduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is what they promised, and this is what they offer. When you contrast that sum with the $128 million by which Mr. Harris reduced taxes a little over a year ago at a time when there was virtually full employment in this country, at a time when the boom was continuing, it is a sad spectacle that we are confronted with.
Turning to the second part of the amendment, about which Your Honour expressed some qualms the other day, I should like to say now what I should have liked to say then, that I did much appreciate the courteous attitude of the Minister of Finance. I think his attitude was wise and just. He suggested that this motion really was about something new, and that was our intention. It was our intention to relate this amendment quite specifically to this disastrous policy, this back-to-Bennett policy of regarding trade as a bad thing, the attitude that you must have a little, but the less you have the better. That is the essence of Toryism.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Dreadful nonsense.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At least when I was a young man the Tories were proud of it. I remember Mr. Arthur Meighen in the Winnipeg rink in 1925-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are sick.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not say 1926. I said "you are sick".

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
