subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a great honour for me to be given the privilege of speaking in this house on behalf of my constituents, and I want to thank each and every one for the support they have given me, and for the confidence which they have placed in me by this mandate.
At the beginning of my speech I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) upon his wonderful address in presenting the budget. I also want to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his cabinet for bringing new hope for greater prosperity to the country by doing everything possible to check the recession, which was brought about by the laissez-faire policy of the previous administration.
I wish also to take this opportunity to pay a tribute to a man who once represented

in this house the riding that I represent today. Many of the older members here will remember the late Senator John T. Hackett. Senator Hackett was a great Canadian. I only wish that I may serve my country as well as he did, and with the same devotion.
Mr. Speaker, I represent the beautiful county of Stanstead, the nicest of them all, in spite of whatever my hon. colleagues in this house may say. The county of Stanstead contains a population of 45,000 inhabitants of whom 33 per cent are English speaking and 67 per cent French speaking, and both these groups live in the best of harmony, in spite of racial issues which were introduced in the last two election campaigns by our Liberal opponents in Quebec. I really think that under the present government and our present Prime Minister there will be greater understanding and unity.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, may I give to the house a picture of my constituency, both from a geographic and economic standpoint.
In the extreme western part of my constituency, there is the fine city of Magog, a tourist centre dominated by Mount Orford and endowed with a national park bordering superb lake Memphremagog, where tourists take pleasure in visiting regularly. Furthermore, Magog has one of the most modern and largest textile plants in Canada. Here I should like to thank the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for all the consideration he kindly gave to the textile problem, and I am sure he will continue, along with the government, to bring new remedies to that industry which is vital to the economy of the province of Quebec and the eastern townships in particular, as well as to that of the country as a whole.
The eastern part of the riding comprises the town of Coaticook, with a population of 7,000. This town also has various industries including a textile plant, though not so large as the one in Magog. Coaticook is, more particularly, a shopping centre for the people of the surrounding fine farming communities.
In the northern part of my riding, Mr. Speaker, there is the town of Lennoxville. It differs from the others in many respects, especially because of its people, who are mostly English-speaking and have a culture very much their own. This is easily understandable, because a nationally known university is located in this area, i.e. Bishop's University, where I had the honour and pleasure, Mr. Speaker, to see an honorary degree conferred on the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker).
Now, Mr. Speaker, coming to the southernmost part of the riding, we find what is called the Three Villages-in French les
The Budget-Mr. Letourneau Trois Villages-which form but one town with the unique distinction of being administered by three different municipal councils. There is first the village of Beebe whose granite quarries are known all over the country not only for the quality of their products but for the modern way in which they are put on the market. I am therefore happy to draw to the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) and of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) to the fact that they can provide all the stone required for the construction of federal buildings in the different parts of the country, even for those which the Minister of Public Works will have to build for my hon. colleague from Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) who, a few days ago, asked the Minister of Public Works to build more harbours and post offices than the preceding government has constructed during its whole mandate.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not correct.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That's the way I took it.
We now come, Mr. Speaker, to the American border where we find Rock Island with its various industries among which is a very large tool manufacturing plant, the only one of its kind, called the Union Twist Drill. This plant has been constructed half on American territory and half on Canadian territory and employs Canadian and American workers who work under the same roof in perfect harmony. This should be an example for the whole world.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with a problem which affects Rock Island as well as the whole area of the Eastern townships and the whole province of Quebec. I mean the construction of a customs and immigration office in that town.
(Text):
Regarding the problem I must tell the house that the Liberal administration has talked about building the customs port at Rock Island for the last 22 years and especially in election years. My predecessor to my personal knowledge used it at least three or four times in order to get himself reelected, but this time it did not work.
The Rock Island customs port is one of the oldest in the province of Quebec. I wish to quote from a publication called "The Customs and Excise Examiner", issue of November 1956:
Prior to 1821, when a port to collect His Majesty's customs was established in Stanstead Plain, there

The Budget-Mr. Letourneau was as far as I have been able to And out, no Canadian customs house nearer than St. Johns, Quebec. So it is no surprise to read in the same Gazetteer of 1824, under the heading of Derby, Vermont, that "This town (Derby) was a port of entry in the late district of Memphremagog, and a collector's office is still kept here by David M. Camp, Esq., Deputy Collector".
This item points to the fact that customs houses may well have been opened first in the United States across the border from this location. This may be further borne out by the fact that Joseph Bouchette, surveyor-general of Lower Canada, in his report of 1815, said:
In the southeast part of the township is the village of Stanstead, which though small has some good houses in it; the main stage road from Quebec into the states of Vermont and New Hampshire, etc., passes through it from which, as bringing a continual influx of strangers some little consequence is derived. From hence the same road leads to Derby in Vermont: at that place communication to almost every part of the United States is easy. To take care of this great traffic a Canadian customs office was opened in 1821 in Stanstead, the first such office anywhere near this area, though another customs office was opened later in East Hereford, Quebec, to cover another stage road up the Connecticut river route.
I have cited these quotations to indicate that for 22 years under a Liberal administration we have in Stanstead, Rock Island, a customs port which has been a disgrace to Canada. It has been shameful to see tourists to Canada having to wait for two or three hours before they could enter the country through this port.
I have some interesting statements concerning the Rock Island customs immigration highway office gleaned from various sources. The first of these is a statement to be found at page 7 of a publication entitled "Travel Between Canada and the United States" for the calendar year 1957 as follows:
Rock Island is one of the largest customs points for the entry of vehicles, in the province of Quebec.
It is the customs port in the province of Quebec having the greatest number of commuters and is the only port in Quebec issuing commuters stickers to speed this traffic. Set right on the main street of the centre of the town and some 100 yards from the international frontier, the customs and immigration office at Rock Island has frequently a tangled web of traffic in front of it during the heavy tourist season or when several trucks awaiting clearance are being held. On some occasions, as with a log jam, some one car has to be released to let things move.
A few years ago-and this must have occurred in an election year-the plan to relieve this congestion was to take the automobile traffic east of the Tomifobia river and, while this was under consideration, three
[Mr. Letoumeau.l
properties were purchased by the Department of Public Works on the east bank of that river. These were the Morel, Clarke and May properties, the latter two being on Church street, Rock Island, and the Morel property being on a lane running from Main street to Church street. The properties were never used for the purpose and have since been resold for a ridiculous amount. During this period at least three suggestions were made and considered to take the traffic off Rock Island's Main street to a customs-immigration office on or near the properties acquired but none managed to meet with the approval of all the municipal, provincial, state and federal authorities involved in the relocation. I have in my hand a brief presented to Mr. Ernest Gohier of Quebec city which outlines this development.
The passage of the national system of interstate highways by the United States in 1956 with a designated throughway, limited access, from Boston and New York to Derby Line, Vermont, adjacent to Rock Island, Quebec, presented a complete change of planning regarding the relocation of the Rock Island customs-immigration office. The period 1956 to the present has seen a closer drawing to agreement of the many governmental agencies concerned in the relocation of the United States and Canadian customs and immigration offices at this key border point.
Automobiles entering Canada on some holidays have lined up in the United States for more than a mile from the port of entry and quite often during the summer months have to be policed both in Derby Line, Vermont, and Rock Island, Quebec, to keep the main streets in both towns open for local business. The traffic varies greatly but I have here exact figures taken from the official records for inward traffic only. As many or more people would be leaving Canada on the same dates. On June 30, 1956, 7,296 persons entered Canada through this port; 6,682 on July 1, 1956; 7,934 on July 2; 7,482 on September 1 and so on. I have placed these few representative figures on the record to indicate the heavy volume of traffic that passes through this port. Year by year the traffic has steadily increased and a large new trucking firm is making arrangements at the present moment for entry of its vehicles through this port. Special chartered buses regularly enter Canada through this port in the summer and it is not an uncommon sight to see anywhere from 30 to 70 people from the buses seeking to use one public toilet now found in the present customs immigration building.

With the new interstate throughway to Derby Line, Vermont, presently under construction in that state and it being understood that the state is ready to complete its section of the throughway from near Newport, Vermont, to the international boundary, it is hoped that the traffic difficulties which have beset the Rock Island customs-immigration officials may be ended before long. I am sure the government will give consideration to my request and that its humble servant will not have to go back to Rock Island and make promises to this effect in order to be reelected next time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the government take every opportunity to help the war veterans. The government could do that by improving the Veterans' Land Act, the Pension Act and by giving the veterans better hospitalization care and attention. I feel that no government will ever be reproached for giving more attention to these men who defended our freedom and liberty.
(Translation):
And now, I would like to suggest to the government that early provision be made for the pegging of family allowances to the cost of living, so that our children may continue to attend school at least until the age of 18. This would not only be of assistance to large families, but would increase the purchasing power of heads of households.
Mr. Speaker, I could hardly refrain from saying a word about the farmers of my constituency, who are an important class there, in numbers as well as in quality. As you know the Eastern townships are particularly suited to dairying, as well as to hog and poultry raising. In the constituency of Stanstead, more particularly, are high class farms of a type rarely seen in other parts of Canada, except out west. There let me congratulate the government for the concern it has shown for the position of the farmer in
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud
Mr. Speaker, I cannot let go unnoticed the feast of Saint John the Baptist, patron saint of French Canadians, which is celebrated tomorrow. On this occasion I extend my best wishes to all the French-speaking Canadians of my constituency, of the province of Quebec and of Canada as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to conclude with these words which I often like to repeat: "Oh Canada, my country, my love, where it is good to live in peace and prosperity!"

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I must confess I am forced to limit my praise and congratulations to the delivery only of the budget speech. In doing this I can see where I am in complete agreement with the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. I can agree also with the first words spoken this afternoon by the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), when he said that nothing spectacular or that no surprise came out of this deficit budget. In fact, he told us that the Prime Minister (Mr! Diefenbaker) had warned the Canadian taxpayers about the coming deficit. As I will mention later in the course of my remarks, this warning was certainly not given before March 31 of this year and even before June 10 of last year.
Tuesday, June 17, 1958, will remain as a blue Tuesday in the history of the Canadian parliament, but it will be a blue Tuesday written in red letters. We had before us after the call of the bells at eight p.m. on that date a Tory Minister of Finance wearing a blue suit, a blue tie, a blue carnation in his lapel, delivering to the astonishment of his blue colleagues and to the other hon. members another one of the historical Tory government deficit budgets.

I would suggest to the government to revise the Canadian farm loan act so that the farmer may borrow substantial amounts of money in order, first, to expand his farm and then mechanize it. It should be realized that today a man can no longer support his family on a 100 or 125-acre farm because with farm mechanization, the farmer needs at least 300 to 500 acres. To that end the farmer would require more credit, on more favourable terms and with a longer period of reimbursement.
If the Conservative members of this house sometimes have the blues when it rains, they definitely had the blues after the Minister of Finance completed the delivery of his first budget presentation. Mr. Speaker, never in the history of the Canadian parliament have so many words been spoken to take away so much from the taxpayers and give so little in return. In fact, it took 46 long pages of Hansard to let the Canadian people know that rat poison would be cheaper and even the ambulance if required could be used at a reduced cost.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How about glass eyes?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Glass eyes come later. And having close relations with poison and the

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud ambulance, we were told that even the flowers would cost less; and I am wondering, Mr. Speaker, whether the pied piper of the Tory party is aware that under a Conservative administration an increasing rodent population is inevitable and could easily invade our idle factories, our closed mining pits and our depressed manufacturing plants to such an extent that a cheap poison would be needed to prevent a disaster resulting from such an undue plague.
After listening the other night to the Minister of Finance and also after listening on Friday afternoon to the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) who was trying, in vain I would say to carry the ball for the government but who unfortunately for them dropped and missed and fumbled, one cannot help but reach the conclusion that the Conservative party may have fooled some of the Canadian people some of the time but all of the Canadian people will not be fooled all of the time.
The 1958 budget will remain in history as a great disappointment to the nation, a budget where the main problem of unemployment has been practically overshadowed by a cloud of mist and uncertainty, a budget where many words were spoken, numerous figures were tabled, but still a budget where confusion, disappointment and unrest prevailed, a budget where even the hopes of the Minister of Finance himself had vanished in illusion and in imagination. It is a budget inconsistent with the policy advocated by the minister and by his colleagues; it is a budget in fact, which by its nature is inflationary and which offers no measure whatsoever to curb or slow down the present trend of inflation which is still threatening the Canadian economy. On page 2009, volume II of Hansard for December 6, 1957, we find the following words:
Having previously forecast a surplus of revenue over expenditure for the year ending March 31 next of $106 million, we may now expect a surplus of $80 million after giving effect to the tax changes that I have proposed.
Those were the words pronounced in this house on December 6, 1957, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). At a later date, on page 4019 of Hansard for January 30, 1958, only two months before the closing of accounts for the last fiscal year, the same minister answered a question addressed to him by the former member for OkanaganBoundary in the following words:
It is not customary to answer questions of that kind or to make interim statements during the course of the fiscal year as to what the expected end result may be of the government's financing for the year. There is not any statement as of May 31, as the question seems to assume. I did give the house a statement on December 6 as to the expected surplus at the end of the current fiscal year.

I want the minister to listen carefully to the next sentence.
I have no reason to depart appreciably from that estimate, and I think at March 31 government operations for the year, thanks to prudent management, will show a respectable surplus.

It must have been rather embarrassing, and I could add almost humiliating, for this great believer of balanced budgets, for this self-appointed protector and custodian of the nation's rights, to have been selected to present the 1958-59 budget, the largest deficit peacetime budget in Canadian history. We are now told by the minister that he is forecasting a deficit of $648 million for the fiscal year. How about the $165 million being liquidated from the national defence equipment account and which, when added to the government's deficit, will make a total of $813 million? On December 6, 1957 the minister predicted a surplus of $80 million, and even as late as January 30 of this year, as I have cited earlier, he stated, and I want to repeat his words:
I have no reason to depart appreciably from that estimate, and I think at March 31 government operations for the year, thanks to prudent management, will show a respectable surplus.
The minister must have had personal and political reasons for his optimism. Those words were uttered when a general election was in sight, and at a time when the minister was refusing to bring down a budget; at a time when it was in the best interests of the hon. gentleman and of his party to hide from the Canadian electors the true facts about Canada's financial situation. After returning to power, and during the last three months, the same government, the same Minister of Finance, this same gentleman who on December 6 last informed this house that no previous minister had ever faced as heavy a

volume of work as that which faced this minister; this same hon. gentleman who on that date very humbly told about the 17 or 18-hour work-day and his 100 hours of work per week; yes, the same minister in the most frank and flowery exposure within the memory of parliament, delivered to the nation the results of his labours, the results of his ambition for power at all costs.
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud Mr. Robichaud: Hon. members can applaud, but while gifts and praise were being showered on the man they said made this Tory political era, while Conservative members, senators and organizers were jubilantly celebrating, what was going on outside? The 1958 budget will remain in history as the Diefenbaker vision at its best. We have in sight what could shape up as the biggest year for new government borrowings since the war years, and the present government may be gradually heading into a situation in which they will not be in a position to practise what they have preached and having to put into effect policies which they claimed to have been so strongly against in past years, particularly since taking power in January of last year. speechtext:
Hon. members must recall that it was during the last Liberal regime, from 1935 to 1957, that the Liberal party led this country with great glory through world war II and it was the Liberal party which, in the post-war period, gave to Canada the greatest decade of expansion and prosperity in its history.
I have just mentioned the improvement of an integrated basis of transportation facilities as an important factor in the solution of the economic problems of the Atlantic region. General recognition of the transportation problem which exists in the Atlantic region is required, as is a long and most complete study of the whole situation. This problem cannot be easily assessed; it could involve rather serious difficulties. It is in fact directly related to the economic development of the whole area and higher government subsidies may not be the answer. Consideration should be given to a more efficient and better integrated system of transportation based upon the economic possibilities of the entire Atlantic region.
On October 18 last the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) said that the bureau of transportation economics operating within his department had been instructed to carry on studies with respect to the transportation problems in the Atlantic region but, on January 30, the only information I could obtain from the minister was that very satisfactory progress was being made with this study. Knowing that the minister never makes exaggerated statements to this house, I inquired of him on May 15 last, seven months after he had announced the study was under way, as to when we might expect a report on the findings of this study. The reply was short and to the point-the study had not been completed. However, on June 10, in reply to a similar question, I received a rather more ambiguous reply from the minister and I will quote his own words as follows:
As no time was set as a target, and as this investigation is a study, it will be carried on until conclusions are reached. It is impossible to give a direct answer to the hon. member's question.

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud
Here is a problem which deserves the immediate and most serious consideration of the government and it is a problem that is considerably aggravating and is substantially contributing to the slow and too modest start in the development of our natural resources.
In view of the immediate importance of this matter, I would suggest the appointment of a special agency, comprised of full-time government officials, which would have specific instructions to study our Atlantic air, water and land transportation systems. Representatives of the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Transport, the Department of Public Works, the Canadian National Railways, the national harbours board and the Department of Finance could share in the work of this agency. Other problems such as the government's purchasing policies, coal policy, the problems of agriculture and fisheries, could also be assigned to this special federal agency. In other words, this would be the group responsible for the co-ordination of the work of different departments, including matters of research, with respect to the Atlantic region.
Such an organization should be assisted by a special Atlantic provinces fund to be assigned for the economic development of the region. The government could set aside the sum of $75 million to $100 million, which at the initiation or suggestion of the provinces concerned, could be used-for say a five-year period-to promote major projects which could in turn ensure the economic progress of the area. A joint capital projects commission under the jurisdiction of the four Atlantic provinces could recommend to the federal authorities or to this agency those projects requiring financial assistance on a priority basis, and the whole Atlantic region would be isolated as a single unit for such a purpose, which would provide for a wide range of federal intervention within these provinces.
I want to make it clear that our oldest provinces should not be regarded as just another Colombo plan area for which the federal government should be asked to vote emergency subsidies. It is furthermore not another area where large interests in the central provinces can look for secondary outlets for their consumer goods or for good market prospects for the disposal of surplus production. What we want in the Atlantic provinces is a fair share of and a participation in the economic growth of Canada; we want to participate through a more diversified system of business activity in the industrial expansion which has so obviously taken place in the last decade in most sections of our country.

There is no doubt that the Gordon commission report, which was followed by concrete measures instituted by the prior administration in co-operation with the efforts of local authorities, created a great psychological effect on the maritime population, resulting in the generation of the confidence and initiative which is so essential for the development of our resources and the expansion of new industries.
The special agency I have suggested-possibly operating under the direction of the Department of Trade and Commerce-could be either a departmental division or a crown corporation whose primary responsibility would be to promote economic development. It has been recognized that the Atlantic provinces do not share the expanding frontiers of other parts of Canada and that something should be done to bring the economy of this vast area in line with those regions.
Once again I wish to remind hon. members that my suggestion should not be regarded as the introduction of a second Colombo plan for the purpose of helping to subsidize a particular emergency program. On the contrary, the people of the Atlantic provinces and the people of other provinces of Canada have witnessed other federal programs such as P.F.R.A., the construction of the trans-Canada pipe line, the St. Lawrence seaway and other projects which have helped certain regions far more than they have helped the Atlantic area. I might say some of these developments have even been detrimental to the Atlantic region, particularly from an economic point of view. The special assistance I have suggested, far from being considered a handout or a charity, could be an effective method of balancing out certain disadvantages which could have resulted from federal intervention in other regions.
Such interventions were needed and have proven beneficial to the areas concerned and the same effects would apply to the Atlantic provinces.
I am not discounting the special grants of $25 million awarded for a period of four years to the four Atlantic provinces as per a formula forming the basis of the equalization principle and being effective as of April 1 of this year. Let us not, however, arrive at the conclusion that these special grants will by themselves solve the problems of those provinces. I hope also that hon. members on the government side are not of the opinion that this particular measure was the first move by Ottawa towards recognizing the needs and requirements of the Atlantic provinces. In looking over the estimates for the fiscal year 1958-59, I find very little in new projects of major importance which could

have favourable and influential reaction in relieving our present unemployment situation. In fact, the largest items in public works estimates are votes specifically designed for the completion of projects originated under the previous administration. It may be advisable to remind hon. members opposite of such projects as the Canso causeway, the Macdonald bridge, the Chatham air base, a number of airports, and the $100 million Camp Gagetown, all projects of major significance which have taken place in the Atlantic provinces in the last ten years.

I am not against the development of the northern section of our country, but again I want to say let us think twice before we launch now, at this crucial period, a vast expansion program at Baffinland, and let us concentrate on areas where the people are unemployed, on areas where vast natural resources are already available and where its development could immediately contribute to the economy of the whole country from coast to coast. Opportunity exists in New Brunswick, and why should the attention of the government be leaning towards the north when our own mines, one of our own basic industries, lie dormant waiting for better days to come. It is important for the maritimes that concrete action be undertaken soon in order to meet the needs of our population by taking full advantage of the possibilities offered from our great untapped reserves.
Mr. Speaker, it may not be too late for the Minister of Finance and the present government to reconsider its attitude and to give practical recognition to our particular problems. Time does not permit me to elaborate further, but in closing I wish to emphasize once more the immediate need for a more concrete study of our transportation problems, for special consideratoin of the possibility of better land use by our farming population, for the creating of a special agency for promoting the development of our natural resources and, finally, the fulfilment of a program which could bring the Atlantic provinces back in a position comparable with the rest of Canada, sharing equally in the country's growth and expansion.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should first like to congratulate the Minister
The Budget-Mr. Broome of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for having done a job which would have stumped any of his predecessors. Previous budgets were rather easy to make because it was only a question of finding a rug large enough to sweep the surplus under. But this budget, where there has to be a careful plan of pump priming and also a continual watch in case of inflation taking over, is a job for an expert and I congratulate the government on having a minister of the calibre of the Minister of Finance.
As the Minister of Finance has stated, we have a paradoxical situation of having at one and the same time a period of recession and a danger of inflation. In this regard I should like to echo the words of the minister when he said that this country must depend on the sense of responsibility of every man and woman not to take more than their fair share of the national income; that increases in income can only be justified by increased productivity, and by increased productivity alone; and that only by keeping our cost of production in line with that of our competitors could we hope to achieve expanding employment and a progressive improvement in our standard of living. The Minister of Finance also emphasized-and this, perhaps, is something new to the members of the opposition-that in respect to all public expenditure we should continue to search for economies and eradicate inefficiency and waste wherever we find them. He asked all members of parliament, regardless of party, to assist him in tracking down waste in every way possible.
We all know how diffidently our friends on the opposite side accepted the offer of the chairmanship of the public accounts committee, which is one major method by which a check can be kept on public expenditure. We also know that on the estimates committee a free rein is given to all members to check as deeply as they wish into the estimates that come before that committee and that is the first time that the committee has had the power, as a standing committee of the house, to do the job that it should be doing.
The budget speech also emphasized that the budget had taken energetic steps to combat the recession. We know that interest rates have declined substantially and that the banks for some time now have had plenty of funds with which to meet all credit requirements. We have been informed that treasury bills are now at their lowest interest rate for many years, and this easing of funds, this change in our monetary policy, has been of tremendous benefit to the country in combatting this recession. Although present investment intentions of business for capital

The Budget-Mr. Broome outlays in 1958 are 11 per cent below the 1957 level, planned outlays for housing, expenditures by government departments and institutional services on the other hand are 14 per cent higher.
I contend that the government acted, and that it has acted with decision. As a result of this action-the measures taken with regard to housing, the increases in pensions, veterans benefits and unemployment insurance-the present recession has taken a much more moderate course in Canada than in the United States to whose economy we are so closely linked. For instance, on a yearly adjusted basis our retail sales are running ahead of last year, while in the United States they are down about 6 per cent. Industrial production in Canada has declined about 5 per cent from its peak, while in the United States the drop is 12 or 13 per cent. Total labour income in Canada has hardly declined at all, while in the United States it is down about 3 per cent. We do not take any satisfaction in the somewhat greater declines in the United States, for nothing could benefit Canada more quickly than an early resumption of business expansion in the United States. But this government is entitled to some credit for the relatively stronger economic position in Canada.
The Minister of Finance expects revenue to be down $387 million and more than half of this reduction, as he pointed out, is due to tax reductions made by this government. However, it is of interest to note that the remaining half of this reduction comes almost entirely from a falling off in corporation profits. Further tax reductions submitted in this budget total $26 million in a full year and these combined with previous tax reductions brought in by this government give a total of $200 million in the way of tax reductions in this government's first year in office.
Although the budget anticipates a record deficit of $648 million the relationship between the net debt as estimated for 1958 and the gross national product is practically unchanged and in fact is lower than the percentage relationship in 1955 or any previous year according to the table included in the budget speech. This percentage relationship was 37 per cent in 1958, 42 per cent in 1955, 44 per cent in 1953 and 47 per cent in 1951. With the exception of the years 1956 and 1957 this is the lowest percentage of the net debt expressed as a relationship to the gross national product.
At this point I would like to express appreciation to the Minister of Finance for the steps that were taken with regard to the revision in the tariff on wood products.
fMr. Broome.]
I wish to quote from the budget speech as recorded at page 1248 of Hansard where the minister said:
Another change relates to the duty on certain lumber products. A recent decision of the tariff board had the effect of classifying many kinds of worked lumber as "manufactures of wood" carrying a higher rate of duty than had generally applied previously. Canadian lumber interests have expressed serious concern about the possible implications of this change for their important export interests and they have been urging that the earlier position be restored.
This budget restored the earlier position which gave United States exporters equality with Canadian exporters to the United States. Considering that we ship more into the United States than we import from that country this is the measure which we on the west coast really desired.
The lumber industry on the west coast accounts for at least 25 per cent of our total payrolls and in certain areas it is the mainstay of entire communities. The position of the lumber industry is dependent to a large extent on transportation costs. Transportation costs to eastern Canada have been skyrocketing in the last few years according to the brief submitted to the transport board by the British Columbia lumber manufacturers' association. This association points out that between April 8, 1948 and January 1, 1957, freight rates have increased from 85 per cent to over 100 per cent. The effect of this has been that rates per 100 pounds Vancouver to Toronto which were 884 cents prior to April 8, 1948 rose to $1.55 on January 1, 1957. If you transfer these rates from the basis of 100 pounds to 1,000 board feet measurements on the basis of 2,600 pounds per 1,000 feet board measure you arrive at a freight rate from Winnipeg to Vancouver which prior to April 8, 1948 was $14.70 increased to $34.60 on January 1, 1957. If it had not been for the action of this government in refusing the latest increase asked by the railways that figure would have risen to $35.90. On the same basis of comparison, Vancouver to Toronto, the rate prior to April 8, 1948, was $22 and on January 1, 1957, it had risen to $40.30.
While freight rates have gone up by over 100 per cent the average selling price f.o.b. mill on coast lumber has on the other hand decreased from $74.28 per 1,000 feet in 1948 to $70.13 per 1,000 feet in 1957. The brief goes on to point out that the British Columbia coast producers being the farthest from the Canadian consuming markets in the prairies and in eastern Canada have of course been hit hardest by these freight rate increases. They point out that in 1948 British Columbia shipped to the prairie provinces 4,330 carloads of lumber. They shipped 1,760 carloads of

lumber in 1957 to this market. They shipped 5,660 carloads to eastern Canada in 1948 and only 3,530 carloads in 1957.
The reason for this of course is that the railroads are caught in a squeeze. A great portion of their traffic comes under bound rates which they cannot change or they will lose the revenue. Also the Crowsnest pass and related rates on grain constitute 27 to 30 per cent of the railroads' volume of traffic and comprises less than 10 per cent of their revenue. In brief the railroads have to have more revenue and they have a limited number of commodities on which they can get that revenue. The answer is not to take away from the grain grower the rates which were given to him at the time the Canadian Pacific railway was put through. It is also not the answer to make a relatively small volume of traffic carry all the extra cost as far as railway operations are concerned. It may be that the railways will be able to hold the line through increased efficiency and complete dieselization. I believe that the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian National Railways are about 50 per cent dieselized at this time.
The lumber industry on the west coast had several other requests of which I will mention only one and that is with regard to forestry expenses. They request that these be made allowable expenses in the calculation of income tax. With respect to depletion they request that it be based on realistic replacement values for the depletion of lumber resources, that is the replacement of timber as it is cut down. They request that it be placed on the basis of the value of the timber at the time of replacement rather than at the time of acquisition. Two of the largest forestry economies in the world, the United States and Sweden, have both realized the significance of this problem and allowed depletion on this basis. I hope the government will take a look at the request of the lumber industry and that it will see fit to meet some of their requirements.
The lumber industry submitted briefs to the tariff board with regard to the proposed increased protection on Canadian steel and steel products and with respect to woollens and worsteds. I took the time to check very carefully into the changes that were proposed by the tariff board. I can assure the hon. member that the changes made in the iron and steel schedule were such as to increase the British preference, if anything, because the previous government had through a multiplicity of end uses-and by that I mean specifying certain end uses of steel imported for that purpose-so changed matters that 57071-3-99
The Budget-Mr. Broome no tariff would apply. Therefore, in effect, the tariff for a great part of the imports was ineffective. Again, the tariff was based on steel at, I believe, six cents a pound. This tariff was set up 15 or 20 years ago. Steel has increased in value to such an extent that the tariff rate at present is not even equivalent to what it was supposed to be at the time it was put on.
As far as woollens are concerned, the increases granted are purely nominal. As far as I can see, the major victory is that we have kept a ceiling of 55 cents to 60 cents a pound and that limits the amount of the tariff that can be paid. I believe the figures given indicate that it will amount to something in the neighbourhood of 20 cents or 30 cents extra cost in the material that goes into a suit of clothes.
While I am discussing our lumber industry, I should like to make reference to the harbour of Vancouver. It may be that some changes should be made in the charges by the national harbours board. In the year 1957 the Vancouver harbour board had a surplus of $1,214,000. Montreal had a deficit of $679,000; Halifax had a deficit of $285,000; and Quebec had a deficit of $1,152,000. Therefore, the deficit of these three ports combined amounted to something over $2 million as compared with an operating surplus in Vancouver of almost $1,225,000. It may be that the charges in Vancouver harbour are perhaps a little excessive or else our operation is a great deal more efficient.
I should like to thank the minister for the changes made in section 35 of the Customs Act which has to do with dumping. In explaining this the minister had this to say, as reported at page 1246 of Hansard:
The present dumping duties section of the customs tariff together with the valuation provisions of the Customs Act are adequate to deal with some forms of dumping. However, they do not deal with cases where goods are being imported into Canada at less than their cost of production and are also sold in the country of export below cost.
The minister said that section 35 was to be amended along the lines of the legislation in effect prior to 1948, requiring that, where appropriate, the value for duty of imported goods shall not be less than the cost of production plus a reasonable advance for selling cost and profit.
I can assure hon. members that this change will be of tremendous advantage, not only to the textile industry of Canada for whom it was developed but also to such people as the Canadian association of equipment distributors who are in the contractors plant and machinery field. I should like to refer to an

The Budget-Mr. Broome article which appeared in the Financial Post, and which reads as follows:
Threat of millions of dollars of cut-price, used U.S. construction equipment flooding the Canadian market grows.
Until now Canadian machinery men have worried mainly about:
Surplus equipment at U.S. bases in Canada.
A build-up in the U.S. itself of privately-owned used equipment.
But now comes word that middlemen may try to unload in Canada huge government-owned stocks under bond in Los Angeles and other cities.
Much of the equipment has come from U.S. foreign defence bases and is prohibited by law from being sold in the U.S.
From U.S. Pacific coast cities: Strenuous efforts are being made by bulk purchasers of government-owned equipment, now under bond, to unload it in foreign markets.
A large movement of it into Canada can be expected if it is not made illegal.
I expect this change in section 35 will take care of something which could completely disrupt the machinery industry on the west coast and, for that matter, throughout Canada.
Would you call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
